titleStmt.title: Liber de natura rerum; or, The Book on the Nature of Things, version Thomas III

sourceDesc.p: Traduction anglaise auto-generee (IA, non relue par un latiniste) a partir du texte latin du corpus zoomathia sous zoo66/2l (Thomas Cantimpratensis, Liber de natura rerum, version dite "Thomas III", recension abregee/remaniee selon la classification textuelle de Konrad Vollmann). Le texte latin source est issu de la base de donnees Sourcencyme (IRHT, dir. Francois Bougard, 2016), encodage TEI par Philippe Pons -- une source academique reputee, non issue d'un pipeline d'encodage automatique par IA, contrairement a d'autres textes du corpus zoo80 (Hippiatrica) traites la meme semaine, ce qui a motive le choix de ce texte comme prochaine cible de traduction. La structure du texte latin source (oeuvre : 6 livres [De animalibus quadrupedibus, De avibus, De monstris marinis, De piscibus, De serpentibus, De vermibus] ; 262 chapitres au total ; 560 citations organisees en <cit> avec <bibl> d'attribution et <quote>) est integralement preservee ci-dessous. Les <note> d'identification moderne de l'encodeur (Philippe Pons), qui ne font pas partie du texte de Thomas lui-meme, ont ete exclues de la traduction, de meme que pour l'extraction du texte latin source. Traduction fournie a titre de meilleur effort ; a verifier par un latiniste avant toute citation savante. Correspond au texte latin deja present dans le corpus sous zoo66/2l.

cit.quote: We must look first, in general terms, at the nature of quadrupeds. Aristotle: animals that have two feet, or four, or none, have blood; but those that have more than four feet do not have blood — this is to be understood of the blood that is carried through veins, for worms indeed have no blood in veins, as lice and fleas do not, since they lack veins altogether, as Pliny says. The general rule is that all sea animals have bony eyes and a tough hide, and this is because salt water would otherwise penetrate anything delicate and soft, and such creatures could not survive unless nature had made them stronger than other animals. In this is signified that worldly people have a mind too hardened toward spiritual things, because the salt of wisdom cannot penetrate them. Aristotle: every animal that has ears has them mobile, except man, and rightly so, since man ought to keep God's commandments fixed in his heart, as it is said to him: 'Write them upon the tablet of your heart!' All animals move the lower jaw except the crocodile and the 'centelia', which move the upper. The tongue is broad or narrow, but a middling one is more praiseworthy, for it suits well-ordered motion better. So do not be given to many words, for 'in much speaking sin will not be lacking,' and so on. Do not be mute like a dog unable to bark. Human eyes are set closer together in proportion to the size of the head than in other animals. Let understanding and affection, or the knowledge of God and of ourselves, therefore be joined in us. Aristotle: every animal that has a hairy tail has a small head and large jaws. Apply this to princes, whose tail — that is, their retinue — is excessive as if hairy, whose head — that is, their judgment — is small, and whose jaw — that is, their voracity — is great. Every four-footed animal with horns lacks upper teeth and has four stomachs; but an animal without horns has only one stomach, like man, the lion, and so on. Hair arises from excess, and excess of humors arises from excess of food. Every animal of much fat has little seed; likewise those fattened by riches do little good. Deuteronomy 32: 'The beloved grew fat and kicked.' No animal of good constitution has much seed — against the lustful. Aristotle: every animal with much hair, and every bird with many feathers, has much seed and much mating. When fat increases, blood diminishes — no wonder, for 'the yoke will rot' before the face of the oil of grace. A body with much blood rots more quickly, whence: 'the beasts of burden rotted in their own dung.' Rennet is found in the stomach of suckling and ruminating animals — that is, in the scriptures — and the older it is, the better it is, and it is good against flux of the bowels, especially that of the hare and the stag. Females are weaker except in the bear and the leopard, as Aristotle says. Among quadrupeds, the female is lighter to train.

Alfraganus: the older rennet is, the better, and the rennet of the small hare and of the stag is good against flux. The same: dog's milk is thicker than any milk except that of pigs and hares. The same: every quadruped desires mating especially in spring. The flesh of all quadrupeds, when they are pastured in watery places, is poor, and an animal with a broad tail bears winter better than one with a long one. Of all females, only the cow has a coarser voice than the male. The same: the horse, the mule, the camel, and the elephant do not have a distinct gall bladder, but veins in which the bile is held. The same: the wolf and the fox bear their young blind.

Aristotle: diviners say that when animals separate from one another it signifies war, and when they follow one another it signifies peace. The same: animals that always dwell in the same place fight one another when their food is scarce — male against female, parents against offspring — and when food is abundant, wild animals return and become tame. The fighting of beasts occurs only for the sake of food and dwelling-place. Those that eat raw flesh fight with all animals, since every animal is food to them. The same: whoever has purer humor has better sense. An animal of much water-content has greater fear, for fear chills the body. A blooded animal, being hot, needs a lung to cool it; a bloodless one does not, since the natural spirit within it suffices. Every hairy animal has viscous seed; thus those who always live in luxury cannot produce pure works. A man with much hair on chin and chest generates more quickly, especially if it is black in color. Every animal with eyelids closes them in sleep, except the hare and the lion. Every wild animal with a serrated row of teeth eats flesh — signifying that princes surrounded by wicked ministers prey upon the poor. Animals with many teeth are generally long-lived; those with few teeth are short-lived. Every animal lacking a lung lacks a voice, but the converse does not hold. No animal ejects seed outside the female vessel, whether waking or sleeping, except man — note in this his baseness. The growth of all animals occurs in that in which they naturally take delight, and what should delight us but our God? All ruminating animals are greatly helped and improved by their ruminating, since they feel in it a certain delight, and these animals fatten more quickly on little food than others that do not ruminate, because of that very delight in rumination. No wonder, for 'the soul that blesses God' — that is, in prayers — 'shall be made fat, and he who inebriates others shall himself also be inebriated.' Every animal lacking a gall bladder lives long, like the elephant, the stag, the camel, and the dolphin — no wonder, for 'the meek shall inherit the land of the living.' Every quadruped has a tail, but man does not; instead he has haunches, that is buttocks, in place of a tail, and what passes into the tail in other beasts passes into the haunches in him — the same reasoning explains why the bear and the ape have no tails, since they have haunches. Animals of large body have little offspring, and those of small body have much offspring, because in large-bodied animals much must necessarily be dissolved away and little of what is superfluous remains. Alas, men of greater dignity produce little fruit! And the reason is that 'the sense given to many things is lesser for each single one.' Every animal that devours its food, like the lion and the wolf, has a lean body, because where there is no chewing of food, food passes badly into transformation. Man is surpassed by many animals in the five senses: the spider is quicker to feel a touch, and so on.

Whence the verse: 'The boar surpasses us in hearing, the lynx in sight, the ape in taste, the vulture in smell, the spider in touch.' Insatiable among animals are those from whose belly food passes through at once, like wolves, stags, and among birds the diving-bird and the pelican — apply this to hearers of God's law who forget it. Man has eight ribs, some have ten; horned animals have thirteen, serpents thirty. Those animals with the longest lifespans are carried longer in the womb, as Pliny says. It is often asked why certain animals ruminate. The solution: fire has a certain property of dissolving what is joined together. Animals, then, that have a hot stomach cook their food easily; animals of cold nature, however, cannot cook their food when they take it in, owing to a defect of complexion, and so they bring it back to the teeth, so that, chewed a second time there, it may more easily be broken down and, once broken down, digested. It is clear, then, that oxen and stags and similar animals are of a colder nature; but these animals have dry, harder, and more solid fat than other animals. Those with hot stomachs signify scholars who, fervent with the Holy Spirit, incorporate the food of sacred scripture into themselves with ease. Hot, on the other hand, are the pig and the sheep, whose fat is softer and more thoroughly cooked. The sheep nonetheless ruminates, though it is of hot nature, but this is because it lacks effective teeth — whence sheep are called 'two-toothed.' Other animals signify the lukewarm, who grasp the secrets of scripture with difficulty, for 'wisdom will not enter a malicious soul.' These, then, have a harder and dry fat, that is, sweetness without devotion. Such creatures fall to the ground rear-end first, because, forgetting the good things to come, they yearn for earthly promises instead.

The ass, as the Book of Nature says, is an animal that knows no discord, a friend of peace and most hardy, gentle under blows, and one that carries burdens without rebelling, even under loads placed on it beyond what it can bear. These are its good qualities. Its vices, however, are these: it is a lustful animal, stronger in its hindquarters than in its forequarters, sluggish, slow of gait, and more brutish and irrational than other animals; walking along a path, it does not know how to give way to one it meets. The foals of asses have some grace in their youth, but the older they grow, the uglier they become.

The milk of the she-ass, as Pliny says, is the whitest, and that whiteness is thought to lend something to the complexion — hence it is found that Nero's wife bathed in ass's milk. The flesh of asses, eaten, produces very poor blood and is digested with difficulty, though it is finer than the flesh of horses. Ass's milk, being warm, strengthens the teeth and eases their pain, especially if they are rubbed with it. It also relieves sighing.

The ass is an animal very much given to cold, and according to Aristotle it fears cold more than other animals. For this reason asses do not mate at the equinox, the season when horses mate, but in summer, so that the birth and generation of the young may occur in warm weather. They carry their young in the womb for a full year. The bones of asses are especially resonant.
As Pliny says, the she-ass rarely bears twins; when about to give birth she flees the light and seeks darkness, so as not to be seen by man.

Whence: 'let not your left hand know what your right hand does.' She gives birth throughout her whole life, which lasts to about thirty years, for 'when a man has finished, then he begins,' and so on. Matthew: 'he who perseveres to the end shall be saved.' They will drink only from springs they are accustomed to, and only the best. Jeremiah 2: 'And now what have you to do with the way of Egypt, that you should drink the troubled water?' — that is, worldly knowledge, which is troubled and dark — 'and what have you to do with the way of the Assyrians, that you should drink the water of the river?' Asses about to cross a bridge, if they can see through to the middle of the river, do not cross it easily.

The wild boar, as the Book of the Nature of Things says, is a strong beast that can never receive any teaching in good conduct, but remains always savage and fierce. It is black in color, and has large curved teeth half a foot long, fit for cutting; in the living beast these can do what iron does, but once drawn from the dead beast they are found to have lost their cutting power. This beast signifies fierce men of the world, who receive no teaching in good works but remain always savage and dark; they have curved teeth in themselves, because whoever wishes to harm another first destroys himself. Their teeth are half a foot long because, though they wound the body, they do not wound the soul. Such men can rage while they live, but not after death. If this animal is attacked by hunters in the morning, before it has voided its urine, it tires easily; but afterward, or while it is urinating, it yields to capture only with difficulty.

As the Experimentator says, warm fresh boar's dung is a chief remedy against nosebleed. If a sow eats many acorns while pregnant, she will miscarry. It is proper to pigs to seek their food by rooting up the earth and to wallow snout-first in mud and filth. A sow's first litter is smaller and weaker than her later ones; when she has many young, her milk is then very scanty.

Among domestic boars, one always prevails by strength and dominates the rest; but if a stronger one comes along, it attacks its predecessor and strives by strength to win the victory. Once this is done, it dominates the rest. At the squeal of one, the whole herd of pigs, running up from everywhere, is roused to a frenzy; that very frenzy is calmed when vinegar is naturally sprinkled on them. Males do not breed past the age of three years. Females are castrated after their mane is cut off, and they fatten more quickly this way. Losing one eye, a pig dies sooner. When a sow has farrowed, she gives the first teat to the first-born. As the moon wanes to its last phase, the brain in a pig is said to shrink more than in any other animal, so much so that, relative to the body, only a small part remains.

The elk, as Pliny and Solinus say, is an animal that grazes on grass moving backward, signifying those who begin from the tail when they ought to have begun from the head, applying themselves to contemplation before struggling against their sins.
The Psalm: 'How do you say to my soul, flee to the mountain like a sparrow,' and it continues: 'for behold the sinners have bent their bow,' and so on.

The 'ahane' is an animal, as Aristotle says, the size of a stag, in which nature has departed from the custom of other quadrupeds. For every four-footed animal has its gall bladder among the internal organs of the belly, except this one. That animal instead has its gall in the ear, and this gall is very bitter and provokes intense anger and ferocity. Apply this to those who listen to slander and twist and corrupt what good they hear.

The buffalo, as the Book of Nature says, is an animal larger than the ox; it has a simple, gentle appearance, but is of the utmost stubbornness and cruelty when provoked to anger. Buffalo milk readily soothes the bowels, heals fresh wounds, and helps those who have swallowed poison. Its gall is medicinal, for it heals the scars of wounds. Mixed with milk it relieves earache. If a heavy load beyond its will is placed on a buffalo, it is at once overcome with fury and throws itself to the ground, and it is not easily made to rise again by blows unless the load that burdened it is lightened. The buffalo draws huge loads under water, yet breathes in the air with the strength of its breath. This animal is also called 'bosontes.'

The bonasus is an animal, as Solinus says, which has the head of a bull, the body and legs of a horse, and horns so tightly curled back upon themselves that, if anyone strikes against them, he is not wounded. When this animal turns to flee, it discharges dung in a stream behind it over the space of a full acre, and the smell of whatever it touches burns; with these weapons it drives off its pursuers. This animal signifies good prelates, who, having the austerity of life within them like horns, do not wound their subjects when they impose that austerity upon them, since they themselves show forth what they preach.

[Basil], on the camel: he says of the camel that it holds a tenacious memory of wrongs and is prone to anger; its grudge is heavy and lasting, and when it has been struck, having long concealed the hurt, it repays the injury the moment it finds the opportunity. It swallows barley quickly and stores it, so as to chew it again by rumination through the whole night.

The Book of Nature says that camels have this compassion, that if one in the herd or in the stable is held back by sickness and does not eat, the others, as though sharing its suffering, abstain as well. At mating time they seek solitude or hidden places.
Pliny: a camel's brain, dried and taken in a drink with vinegar, cures epilepsy, that is, the falling sickness.
Solinus: camels do not accept loads beyond what is just. A camel's young, as soon as it is born, feeds itself in the meadow.

Aristotle: a certain man covered a camel's mother with a cloak, so that the camel would mate with her without recognizing that she was his mother, and before he finished the mating, he uncovered her and killed the one who had devised the trick; for a camel by nature detests mating with its mother and the sight of men during its mating, since its mating is done from behind.
Solinus: camels are so maddened by desire for mating that they grow savage.

Dogs, as Jacques says, are beasts teachable in every kind of sport; although they willingly sleep, they nevertheless guard their masters' homes while keeping watch. They love their masters so much that they sometimes meet death for their sake. Solinus: dogs alone among animals understand their own names. Jacques: there is also a certain breed of dog that recognizes thieves by scent and distinguishes them from other men with an implacable hatred. A dog's blood, given to another sick animal, restores it to health. When dogs lie beside their masters' table, according to Jacques they arrange themselves so that with one eye they watch their master's generous hand, and with the other they can see the door.

The attack and savagery of dogs, as Pliny says, is calmed by a man crouching down to the ground. Pliny: dogs bear blind pups and carry them for sixty days. During mating the two remain locked together, and this comes from an excess of ardor in their lust. The best of a litter is the pup that begins to see last, or the one the mother first carries to the den. All dogs are born blind and remain blind for twelve days, though some for as much as three months. A dog's rabies is calmed by mixing cock's-comb honeycomb into its food. The root of the wild rose treats their bite, for their bite, when they are rabid, is deadly. Dog's milk is thicker than any milk except that of the sow and the hare; they have milk in their teats for seven days before giving birth. When one dog, hurt, cries out, the rest, indignant, set upon it with their teeth. Note that in every kind of animal males live longer than females, except in the breed of greyhounds, and this because of the toil they undergo.

Sick dogs eat, as Aristotle says, a certain herb of a foul taste, so as to vomit up the harmful humor and be healed. Aristotle: a dog's age is not easily known except by its teeth, for in the young they are sharp and white, in the old, black and blunt. Many have said that a dog cannot live except among men, and is driven to madness if kept away from human habitation. A dog's tongue is medicinal, and by licking heals its own wounds and those of others. Male dogs do not readily harm females, and this holds true in many kinds of beasts, God in His wisdom having so ordained it among brute animals, so as to show that among rational creatures there ought to be concord, and that the male sex ought to spare the weaker sex. It is a most unworthy habit of dogs to foully befoul the loveliest and greenest places. Shoes made of dog-hide cure gout, though if dogs catch their scent, they will urinate on them. Whether a bite is from a rabid or a non-rabid dog is known as follows. Philosophus: a plaster made of well-pounded walnut and placed over the wound for a day and a night should then be given to a hungry cock or hen. If it drinks after eating it, the bite was not from a rabid dog; if it does not drink, it will die, though not necessarily at once — sometimes it is delayed a day and a night. Likewise, if it was a rabid dog's bite, bread dipped in the blood flowing from the wound will not be eaten by a healthy dog. A remarkable thing: an animal bitten by a rabid dog sometimes licks its own pups and barks.
Alexander: it is sound advice to leave a wound open for a year, so that it not be closed over by scar tissue.

The beaver ['castor'] is named from castrating, and its testicles are called 'castoreum.' It vomits up its gall, as Pliny says, which is useful for many medicines, and it is for this reason that it is believed to pursue itself. Its rennet calms the falling sickness. This animal cannot long survive unless it keeps its tail in water, which indeed resembles the tail of fishes. Castoreum warms and dries, and has the property of thinning the vital spirit of those who suffer spasms. It is most useful for tremors of the limbs arising from a defect of the sinews. The fat of the membranes of its testicles and groin is of great value for the same purposes. Wine boiled with castoreum, and the scent of castoreum itself kept near a man suffering paralysis, is an incomparable remedy.

Goat's milk is the sweetest, but as soon as it curdles it spoils. Goat's milk, after human milk, is the most temperate. Cheese made from goat's milk is of no use at all, as Aristotle says. Goats become sterile from fatness, and also miscarry when exposed to cold. The wild she-goat is a most cunning animal, loves high mountains, and recognizes from a distance whether approaching men are hunters or travelers. Goats are said to breathe through their ears, not their nostrils, and never to be free of fever. The eyes of the he-goat look sideways because of its lust. They see equally by night as by day, and so goat's liver, if eaten, restores night sight to those the physicians call 'night-blind.' The gall of the he-goat, applied to the eyelids, wastes them away; it heals cloudiness and blockage of the eyes. If you place he-goat's gall somewhere, it will draw frogs to itself. Aristotle nonetheless says that he-goats are often blinded by day and do not see well by day, but their sight sharpens at night. A goat's horn, burnt, if held before the nostrils of one who is truly epileptic, makes him fall at once; it also puts serpents to flight. The freshly shed, warm blood of the he-goat is of such power that it can shatter a diamond, which no metal can overcome.

Goats, as Pliny says, live on poisonous plants and do not die from them; but they say goats die if made to swallow honey. Their bite is deadly to a tree. By licking an olive tree they render it barren. When wild goats are struck by an arrow, they eat the herb pennyroyal in order to draw the arrow from the body.

The wild she-goat, called 'capreola,' or 'rabicapra' as Pliny calls it, is a beast fierce toward its own kind, but timid and very gentle toward other beasts. There is great discord among the males, and this on account of the females at mating time.

Cacus is a monster in Arcadia. This animal is entirely bristled like a pig, and, as the philosopher Adelinus writes, belches flames from its chest — that is, breath and a fiery exhalation — and it does this especially when moved to anger.
Similar to these animals are those of whom it is said in the Book of Wisdom that 'fire breathed from their mouths.' Apply this to angry slanderers or old procuresses.

No animal, as Aristotle says, sheds its horns except the stag. All horns are hollow except the stag's, which are solid, with no cavity in them. This animal boasts exceedingly of its horns. When stags feel themselves weighed down by sickness or age, as Pliny says, they draw serpents from their lairs with the breath of their nostrils; and having devoured them, driven by the burning poison they seek out a spring, and after drinking the water they recover their youth. Solinus: it has never been observed that a stag runs a fever, and for this reason ointments made from their marrow calm the heat of feverish men. The females separate themselves from the males at the time of conceiving; before giving birth they purge themselves with a certain herb called 'seselis,' which eases the womb for what follows. Solinus: they bear twin young, which they carefully hide, and, once hidden among the bushes, they train them with blows on the legs to lie still until they mature. The flesh of fawns killed in their mother's womb effectively drives away poisons and heals snakebite. When pursued by dogs, they turn to face the barking, and so direct their path downwind, so that the sound of the dogs may fall behind with them. A steady diet each morning of their flesh keeps one free from fevers for life. They seek the sun, as Aristotle and Pliny say, and stand in it when their horns are fresh, so that they may ripen and dry in the sun's heat and become strong; and afterward they go to trees and rub themselves there, testing their horns, and then go out unafraid, since they now have weapons, whereas during the time of the change in their horns they hid for fear of wolves and fed only by night, as though unarmed. In water, however, they shed their horns, so as to keep them hidden from human use there, out of a kind of jealousy, knowing them to be useful for medicines, especially the right horn. A special remedy for driving off serpents is the smoke of a burnt stag's horn, whether left or right.

Platearius: in the stag there is a certain bone that serves as a support, as in other members. This bone, extracted from the stag and hardened like true bone though it is cartilaginous, is powdered and given to the sick for heart trouble and fainting spells.

Some say that stags have their gall in the tail, others in the ear, as Aristotle says. The intestines of stags are very foul-smelling, and Pliny holds the reason to be that the gall lies within the intestines, which dogs so abhor that they will not eat them unless famished. In its head there lives a single worm, which almost constantly torments it. But every animal, and man himself, has a worm under the tongue; and in that part of the body where the veins lie near the vertebra joined to the head, there are twenty worms in number. Stags fear the voice of foxes. Male stags fight one another, and the victor rules over many in a single pasture, while the defeated obey the victor with great submission, and so, subject to one lord, they live in peace among themselves. When a fawn is caught by a man and led a little while in bonds, it will follow the man even when unbound afterward.

As the Experimentator says, the flesh of the stag is melancholic and hard to digest. The fawn, which is the stag's offspring, has better flesh; and if the fawn is castrated its flesh will be even better, since it will be more temperate in heat and moisture. Stags marvel at every kind of harmony, so much so that, if hounds have broken loose, they can be lured back into danger by sweet baying.

The 'cyrogrillus' is an animal forbidden in the Law. It is a small and by nature weak animal, and it is remarkable in this, that although it is weak, it is nonetheless troublesome, rapacious, and deadly to the other creatures of the earth.

The 'cathapleba' is an animal, as Pliny and Solinus write, living near the river Nile, so deadly to look upon that whoever meets its gaze immediately loses his life. This is the concupiscence of the eyes.
Matthew 6: 'whoever looks upon a woman...'

The 'corocrates' is a beast, as Solinus and Jacques say, which imitates the voices of men as the hyena does; it never closes its eyes. In its mouth there is no gum, but a single, everlasting tooth which, so that it is never blunted, naturally closes like a little box. This tooth has such power that it can grind up anything at once. This beast is said to be conceived from a dog and a she-wolf.
The doe or 'dammula' is an animal, as Isidore says, so called because it slips away from the hand.

For it is a timid and feeble animal, of which Martial says: 'the boar defends itself with its tusk, horns defend the stag; what are the defenseless does, but prey?' Apply this to those who through cowardice do not resist the devil the tempter.

The 'duran' is an animal, as Aristotle says, cruel, swift, and very strong. When this animal is pursued by dogs and hunters and begins to break under despair, seeing that it cannot escape, it hurls dung behind it at the pursuing dogs with a natural cunning, slowing them down with the stench and filth of its droppings. Apply this to those who overcome preachers with the filth of worldly things, so that they cannot bring them into the Church.

The badger, as the Book of Nature says, is an animal the size of a fox. Its fat grows as the moon waxes and shrinks as it wanes, so much so that if it is killed at the very end of the moon's wane, no fat at all is found in it. Ointments made from its fat relieve pain of the kidneys and injuries of the limbs, and this is remarkable, because this beast, although in one respect medicinal — namely as regards its fat — is nonetheless most deadly and grievous in its bite.

The elephant is tamed more quickly than any other animal, nor is any other wild creature so domesticated and obedient to man among all the wild animals. They are strong in memory, hence they readily receive instruction and the discipline of manners. Many animals, as Aristotle says, retain memory of what they see or learn — true, this, of the memory of judgment. Only man, however, has discernment and possesses intellectual memory. The taming of the elephant is well known — namely, how it is domesticated by torment and by seizure. When about to cross a river, the smaller ones are sent ahead, lest the larger ones wear down the riverbed and create deep, sunken channels. Between elephants and dragons there is a constant enmity. Out of modesty they mate only in hiding.

As Pliny says, they do not return to the herd's company until they have washed in running water. They never fight over females, since they know no adultery. The female about to give birth enters a deep pool, for if the offspring fell to the ground it would be unable to rise. After the female gives birth, she rests for three years; once a female is pregnant, she is never again touched by the male, and she carries the young in the womb for two years.

Solinus: they mate over two days at a time, and no more than that in a year. They fear mice and flee them, being troubled by their stench. Their backs are extremely tough, their bellies softer. By the smoke that comes from an elephant's groin and hide, every venomous creature is put to flight.

The Book of Nature says that in their youth they can bend their knees, but not in old age, when they grow stiff. The young sometimes lift up a falling elder with their trunk. They suffer pain of the joints, for which a drink of cold water and grasses steeped in honey are of use to them. By nature it gladly drinks wine. It grows for forty years, and then it feels cold and winter and the chill wind. They live three hundred years; they are utterly unable to bear cold.

Jacques: whence ivory, which is made from their bones, is cold and white. For if a cloth is laid upon ivory, and fire set upon the cloth, the cloth is not burnt, since the natural coldness of the ivory extinguishes the fire.

Solinus: they harm only when provoked. They kill flies settling on their backs by contracting the skin into wrinkles; this serves them in place of a switching tail. And note that their intestines are so arranged and formed as to be a defense against all the animals of the earth.
Aristotle nonetheless says that the inward parts of the elephant resemble those of the pig, and by extension those of man. The burnt bone of an elephant drives away poison and serpents.
Elephants roused to battle by the sight of the blood of grapes lose all their fighting spirit entirely if a pig comes before them grunting.

Among horses, the more spirited and high-strung one plunges its muzzle deeper when drinking. Isidore: in every animal that advances in age, the teeth blacken, except in the horse, whose teeth whiten as it ages; hence its age is read from its teeth. In horses especially, and in every kind of draught animal, the ears reveal the state of the mind: drooping in the weary, twitching in the fearful, pricked up in the eager, relaxed in the sick. The horse alone among animals, along with the cow and the stag, has cartilaginous bones in the heart, and this because of its size, so that the heart may be supported by these bones as it is in other members; but only the stag's such bone is medicinal. Mares have such great affection that if one of them dies in the herd, another mare will nurse the dead one's foal as her own. Horses by nature love their own kind more than other beasts do.

Alexander: noble horses are said to foretell their master's death by a flood of tears. Only the horse, besides man, is known to weep and to grieve beyond measure for its dead master, so much so that, refusing to eat, some die of hunger.

Aristotle: man and horse love mating more than other animals. A certain king had a beautiful mare, and from her a beautiful colt. Wishing to breed the colt to his own mother, he covered the mare's face so that the colt, that is, her own son, would mount her. When this was done, the horse recognized his mother, and fleeing, threw himself down and died. Another horse, after recognizing his own mother, tore out his own genitals and threw himself down. Philosophus: from a horse's tail-hair, left in water, a worm is generated within a few days.

The dromedary is a kind of camel, as Hrabanus says, smaller in size but much faster than the camel. Hence its name, from 'dromos,' which in Greek means 'running' or 'speed'; for it runs a hundred miles or more in a single day. This animal ruminates.

The hedgehog, as the Gloss says commenting on the passage where unclean animals are forbidden in the Law, is also called by another name, 'cyrogrillus.' It is a spiny animal shaped like a little pig; except on its belly it is entirely enclosed in spines, as a defense against ambush.

The Experimentator says of the hedgehog that the nourishment of its body passes into its spines because of the scarcity of its natural heat. Hedgehog flesh has a drying and dissolving property; it specifically strengthens the stomach, loosens the bowels, and provokes urine. It is useful for those disposed to elephantine leprosy. The hedgehog alone has two anal openings, through which it passes its waste.
The ash of a burnt hedgehog, mixed with melted pitch, restores hair to a scar, as Pliny says.
Aristotle: the hedgehog mates with the female standing, and this because of the spines on its back.

The 'falena' is an animal born in remote parts of the world, given and created for the punishment of proud men. For this animal, out of a certain natural indignation, detests pride in man, and, if it finds occasion to engage, presses on relentlessly to the fight, and, as the victor over pride, strives mercilessly to tear men apart. But conversely, if it perceives in a man it meets some sign of humility through flight and fear of humiliation, it sometimes stops and lets him escape.

The 'furunculus' is an animal we commonly call the ferret, exceedingly spirited, and it burns with more heat than nature gave it strength for, a little larger than the weasel. They are said to mate lying flat. If a female has no male, when driven by lust she swells up and dies.

The 'furion,' as Aristotle says, is a lustful animal; it gorges itself on food and for this often runs into danger. Because of this excess it cannot long endure, since this excess forbids it. This animal practices the act of lust with more intemperance than others; its lust follows from its excess in eating. When it mates, it rises up and is shaken almost as if in a raging fit over the female, and when it cannot complete the mating it so intemperately craves, it cries out and is agitated during mating. Indeed, in every animal nature forbids much mating, though desire for lust craves much of it. For seed is the strength of blood violently expelled in mating; hence whoever exceeds the proper measure in mating is cheated of his due strength and hastens his own death before its time. It is often heard that a man suddenly dies in the act of mating, and this because too burning a desire drains and destroys the vital spirits. So then, this animal, the 'furion,' is seen to mate in the manner of men. For the male mounts from above, and the female, lying beneath, is equal to him under him. It never changes this order, though man himself, the most orderly of all animals, changes the order of his own nature, mating from behind like a dog, or standing like a hedgehog, or with the female above — which is the most shameful crime in any living creature; for no animal but man is found to do this.

The dormouse, as the Book of Nature says, is a small animal; it sleeps through the whole winter, lying curled up in a ball, and, remarkably, as Isidore says, it fattens from that very sleep. It runs about in trees as it does on the ground, and delights greedily in the juice of fruit.
A decoction of dormouse, Pliny says, and anointing the limbs with it, will help those who fear paralysis.

The 'gali,' as Aristotle says, is an animal of great daring; it fights with serpents and, once it has beaten them, eats them, and then at once eats rue, which is hostile to serpents. The chief reason it fights with serpents is that this kind of serpent lives on the flesh of mice, and the 'gali' itself likes to eat mice; so it pursues serpents as rivals for its own food.

The 'guessides,' or 'roserula' as it is commonly called, is an animal that dwells often near water; it produces dung that is remarkably fragrant, resembling musk in scent, though unequal to it in strength and intensity. And this is remarkable in the beast: it gathers its dung in one place, as though showing that it does not begrudge man, but sets its good gift out ready for anyone to take. It flees the sight of men; by which indeed we are shown that, in doing good, we should avoid the sight and praise of men.
Ibexes are beasts, as Galen says, small of body, dwelling among rocks, where they also bear their young.

cit.quote: [stags]
'ibex' in the nominative case, whence the verse: 'the ibex is an animal, the ibis a bird, and the ibis is envious,' namely from 'eo, is, it' [to go].

The 'ibrida' is a four-footed animal of mixed kind, that is, born of different species, as Isidore says. Just as the mule comes from the horse and the ass, so the 'hybrida' is born from wild boars and domestic pigs; the 'titurus' is born of a sheep and a he-goat, and the 'musino' of a she-goat and a ram.

The porcupine, as Solinus says, is a beast commonly called the spiny pig. It dwells near the sea, and thrives equally well on land and in water. Its back bristles with quills, which, when it vigorously releases them, it shoots at will, wounding dogs or men who draw near.
Its anger, as Jacques says, is very quick to seek vengeance.

The hyena, as Pliny and Solinus say, is an animal that dwells always among the tombs of the dead. It has two natures, that of female and that of male. When its spine stiffens, its neck cannot be bent without turning the whole body around. Hunting dogs, if they so much as touch its shadow, lose their voice and cannot bark. It changes color at will. Whatever animal it circles about becomes transfixed in its tracks; it bears a precious gem in its eyes, or according to some, in its forehead. It is the size of a wolf; on its neck it has hairs like those of a horse's mane, and it has the coarsest hairs of all, which Pliny calls its 'spondylia.'

It follows the stables of horses, according to Aristotle and Jacques. By constant listening it learns to imitate a name well enough to reproduce the sound of a human voice, so that it may lure a man out by cunning trickery and kill him. It mimics human retching with false gasps, and so lures and devours dogs that come to investigate.

The lion, as Jacques and Solinus say, is the king of the animals; it lacks guile and suspicion. A lion's disposition is shown by its brow and tail. They are of such hot nature that they are said to mate at every season. The lioness bears five cubs the first time, four the second, three the third, two the fourth, and only one the fifth time, after which she becomes barren. She has only two teats, in the chest, in the middle of the belly, and these are small, not proportioned to the size of her body, and the reason for this is the small quantity of her milk, since her food passes into her own body.
Augustine: when she gives birth, the cub is said to sleep for three days, until it is roused, trembling, by the roar of its returning father.

Solinus: a lion, unless injured, is not easily angered, but when it is deliberately provoked, it utterly crushes its opponent; it spares those laid low, and lets captives who cross its path go free, and kills a man only under great hunger, as the Book of Nature says.
When it sleeps, as Adelinus says, its eyes stay watchful; when it walks, it covers its tracks with its tail, so as not to be found by hunters.
As Pliny says, the ferocity of lions does not turn against one another, but among themselves they are peaceable.

Aristotle: the lion, like a dog, lifts its leg when it urinates; when it opens its mouth, a strong odor comes forth from it. When hungry, it drags its tail over the ground in a wide circuit, and by roaring frightens off animals, which do not dare cross the swath its tail has marked. It scorns yesterday's food and even shuns the leftovers of its own meal.
[A lion] is destroyed and consumed inwardly by its own rage's fiery blood, when its fury knows no measure. The lion hunts the wild ass and hates it by nature.
A sick lion, as Ambrose says, seeks out an ape to devour, so that it may be healed. A lion, having drunk the blood of a dog, is cured of its sickness.

Solinus and Pliny: a lion flees the scorpion's sting as an enemy. It fears the noise of wheels, but fire even more. Its tail is still when it is being coaxed and gentle, which is rare; at the start of its anger its tail lashes the ground, and as its anger increases, it whips its own back. Wounded, it recognizes with remarkable perception the one who struck it, and picks him out in however great a crowd; but the man who threw a weapon and missed, it seizes, whirls around, and throws down, without wounding him. Pliny: the flesh of the lion, and especially its heart, gives warmth to those who eat it, and is therefore given as a remedy to those weakened by cold. Its bones are so hard that fire can be struck from them as from flint. The fat of the lion is opposed to poisons. A man anointed with wine and lion's fat drives off all wild beasts, and even puts serpents to flight. Its fat is warmer than that of any other quadruped. The lion is nearly always feverish, with a quartan fever, and it is then that it especially craves the flesh of the ape, so as to be cured. Lion's fat with oil of roses guards the face from blemishes, brightens the complexion, and heals it. The bone of its neck is a single continuous piece, but the flesh of its neck is cartilaginous and almost like a single sinew, whence it cannot bend its neck backward or to the side.

Alexander: the lion has great strength in its chest and forelegs, and in its tail. It is called 'leo' from the Greek 'leon,' which means 'king' in Latin, since it is the king of beasts. The lion is of hot nature in its forequarters and cold in its hindquarters; so too is the sun when it is in the sign of Leo.

Aristotle: in the lion alone there is no marrow in any bone except the thigh bone; for this reason its bones are harder than those of any other animal except the dolphin. Its whole interior resembles that of a dog. It runs a fever in every summer, but is healthy in winter. A lion runs a fever from merely seeing a man.
The leopard, as Solinus says, is an animal born of the lion and the panther. The females of these are bolder and stronger than the males.
Pliny: anyone wishing to withstand a raging leopard should rub garlic between his hands; without delay the leopard will recoil and offer no resistance, since it cannot bear the smell of garlic.

Ambrose: a leopard afflicted with an internal sickness drinks the blood of a wild goat and so escapes the force of its illness. When it has eaten something poisonous, it seeks out human dung, and, eating it, is cured. Leopards are sometimes tamed, but never so fully that they forget their own cruelty; they are, however, tamed for hunting. So when it is led out to hunt, it is released upon the prey. If it fails to catch it within four or five leaps, it stops, fiercely enraged, and unless the hunter at once offers the raging beast something whose blood may appease it, it attacks the hunter or whoever else is nearby, since it cannot be appeased except by blood. But those who always keep lambs or other animals on hand to appease it with are prudent in this. Some believe the leopard and the 'pardus' to be the same beast, differing only in name.

The 'lamia,' as the Book of Nature says, is a large and most cruel animal. By night it leaves the forests and enters gardens, breaking trees and scattering their branches, and this with arms of exceeding strength, fit for any task or action.

A man wounded by the teeth of the 'lamia,' as Aristotle says, is not healed of the bite until he hears the roaring beast's voice. This beast is most ferocious, yet offers its teats and suckles its young when they beg for them. Crueler than these beasts are prelates who do not break the bread of the Spirit for their little ones, and who hinder others who would.

The 'lanzani' is an animal, as Solinus and Jacques say, most savage, from whose cruelty no beast can be safe. For, they say, it terrifies even the lion, who is himself feared by all. It preys upon beasts not of its own kind, but spares its own kind. Yet it pursues with implacable hatred those animals that prey upon other beasts, and, though it punishes this crime in others, it does not recall its own wickedness. It pursues man in a remarkable way, and this perhaps by God's own will, so that the creature that ought by nature to be the gentlest of all animals is instead the most savage, through the malice of its own vicious wrongdoing.

The wolf is a deceitful and most rapacious animal. Near the sea it tears apart fishermen's nets laid out to dry, unless they leave it fish where it lies. Experimentator: it gathers willow leaves in its mouth and hides beneath them, so as to catch goats that come to eat the leaves. When a wolf walks among leaves, so as not to be detected by the sound, it licks its own feet with its tongue and so makes them slick and moist, so as not to be heard by dogs. When a wolf enters a sheepfold, not content to satisfy its hunger with a single strangled sheep, it strangles all it can. A wolf's fleece teems with worms.
Aristotle: not only its blood, but also its dung, is beneficial in cases of bilious disease.
The wolf has poor sight, seeing more clearly by night. Pliny: if a wolf senses it has been seen first by a man, it loses its ferocity, for it no longer has its usual vigor and speed in running.

Ambrose: if a wolf catches sight of you before you see it, it takes away your voice, and if you have fallen silent, undo your cloak, so as to loosen your speech. If a wolf attacks you, it flees toward a rock. If it follows you gradually from behind, meaning to ambush you, while it watches, place some object between you and it, and, fearing entrapment, it will stop. No flesh-eating animal but man and the bear eats plants with impunity. A wolf, having tasted the sweet flavor of human flesh, which is more delicate than any other flesh, seeks to eat it again, and, enticed by the sweetness of that flesh, does not fear the danger of attacking man. It is proper to wolves to fear fire. The same remedy applies to a wolf's bite as to that of a rabid dog, since the same poison issues from both. A wolf passing secretly through a hedge to ambush sheep, if it happens to make a noise with its foot, at once bites that foot as though it were guilty. A wolf's brain is said to grow and shrink according to the phase of the moon, and although this happens in all quadrupeds, it is more pronounced in the wolf than in any but the dog, in which nature has granted the same. A wolf's heart, burned and reduced to ash and given in a drink, is said to help epileptics, provided the patient is not afterward stained by any lechery.
A wolf's heart, if dried and preserved, is said to become very aromatic, as the Experimentator says.

The 'lincisius' is a four-footed animal born of the mixture of a dog and a wolf, the mother being a she-wolf and the father a dog. For each parent is so lustful that, though the natural hatred between dog and wolf opposes it, they nonetheless come together in mating for the sake of lust's pleasure, and so it happens that the offspring draws to itself the temperament and habits of both parents. These beasts are strong and extremely fierce.

The 'leocofana' is a small beast, as Solinus and Jacques say, which, once captured, is burned, so that its ashes may be scattered on the paths of lions. So too, by humility and the example of the converted, may the paths of the proud be sprinkled. For lions die if they so much as touch a little of these ashes; on this account lions pursue this beast with a natural hatred, and, once caught, tear it apart, but are themselves rendered lifeless from the very bite. So this creature, against an approaching lion, sprays its urine, knowing this to be deadly to it.

The hare rarely goes out to graze except at night, being a timid animal. As Pliny attests, it never grows fat. The weasel is said to play with the hare in sport, and when it sees the hare grown weary from play, seizes its throat with its teeth, grips it fiercely, and, having killed it, eats it. A domesticated hare, when it lacks movement, develops fat over its kidneys and dies. A hare's lung, placed on the eyes, heals them, and when crushed and applied, heals tired feet. Its rennet is good against flux of the bowels. Its hind legs are longer, so that it climbs a hill more easily than it descends one. It sleeps with its eyes open.

The otter, as the Book of Nature says, is a cunning and malicious animal. It dwells near ponds and rivers, is the size of a cat, and almost the same shape except for its head. Though it can live long under water, it nonetheless draws breath from the air. Hence it sometimes happens that it enters a fish-trap made of woven wicker for the sake of prey; but, unwilling to leave its catch behind and unable to return by the way it entered because of how the trap is built, it must in the meantime drown in the water, since it cannot draw breath from the air. Some call this device a 'nassa.' This beast is so avaricious and greedy for food that it gathers caught fish in its den, where it lurks, in so great a heap that, from the excessive stench of decay arising from the rotting fish, it pollutes not only the den but even the air; something some men have learned, not without danger to themselves.

The lynx, as Pliny and Jacques say, is a beast with eyes so piercing that its keen sight is said to penetrate solid bodies. It has a tongue like that of serpents, though larger, which it stretches out to great length. Its urine is said to solidify into a precious stone called 'lyngurium.' But out of a certain natural envy it hides, as much as it can, the liquid it discharges, so that such waste does not come to our use. This stone eases pain of the kidneys and heals jaundice.

The locust is a four-footed animal, as Jacques says, found in the eastern regions near the Jordan; it is quite small, but has a large head, fleshy and edible. Hence it is read in the Gospel that John the Baptist fed on these.

The locust travels in swarms; hence in Proverbs: 'the locust has no king, and yet it goes forth all together by troops' — which cannot be said of the locust-worm, since these do not go forth in troops but singly.

Aristotle seems to speak of these; for he says that a certain woman raised a locust from the time it was small, and when it had grown, found it pregnant of itself, without a male. In which it appears that the locust is a four-footed animal, and that the female sometimes generates by herself without a male.

The mule, as the Book of Nature says, is an animal outstanding in strength for labor, born of the adulterous mixing of the seed of the ass and the horse. A mule's tendency to kick is restrained by frequent draughts of wine. From an ass and a mare comes the mule; from a she-ass and a horse, the hinny.

The mastiff is a very large beast, as Adelinus says, which, though it charges boldly and fiercely at all who cross its path, nonetheless shrinks in dread from the innocence and smallness of children and flees their blows.

The musk-deer is a beast of the East, as Pliny says, the size of a roe deer, in whose groin an abscess grows, formed from its humors. When this has ripened, the animal strikes and rubs it against a tree, and from this rubbing the abscess bursts, and the discharge runs down there, congeals, and hardens, and this substance is called musk. All its flesh, and even its dung, is called musk, but that which flows from its abscess recovers its lost scent when placed among foul odors and latrines. It is good against fainting and weakness of the heart, of the brain, the liver, and the stomach.
The 'musio,' or cat, called in Greek as it were 'the cunning one,' as Jacques says. It sees keenly.

As the Experimentator says, at mating time it readily turns wild. They fight one another most fiercely, especially to keep their accustomed hunting grounds. Around their mouths they have long whiskers, which, if removed, cause them to lose their boldness. A domestic cat, when it begins to turn wild, should have its ears clipped; unable then to bear drops of dew in its ears, it will be forced to return to the shelter of the house. It is so drawn by love toward its own kind that, if it stands over a well and sees its own shadow in the water, thinking to enjoy the company of one like itself, it will fall of its own accord from the height into the depths. This happens above all when a female, seeking a male, is more ardently inflamed with desire, and especially in young cats, who have less knowledge of danger.
The weasel, as the Book of Nature says, is as though called 'mus-tela,' the 'long mouse'; for 'telos' in Greek means 'long' in Latin.
There are two kinds, as Isidore says, the greater and the lesser, which is called the 'ictis.' When it wishes to fight with serpents, it arms itself with wild rue. It hunts mice and serpents.
Solinus says that it kills the basilisk, which kills men by sight alone and other animals by its very breath. Yet once the basilisk is killed, the weasel also dies.

Its gall is effective against the asp; the rest of it is poison, as Pliny says. The weasel, in the houses where it raises its young, often moves them, changing their location, so that they will not be found. It is a skilled hunter of mice, and is also quick to avenge its own injuries.

[Elephants] are troubled by the smell of mice. Aristotle: a mouse dies if it drinks water, and this because it is of a very moist nature. Mouse dung strongly loosens the bowels, whence vagabonds take a remedy from it.

And note that Pliny speaks of the Libyan mouse, which does not drink water, and perhaps not of every mouse generally. A mouse, finding many cheeses in one place, tries them all and eats whichever it finds best. Mice utter sounds at the full moon, and are silent at the new moon, as Pliny says. These creatures are harmful when driven by lust, so that if their urine touches a bare part of a man, it makes his flesh rot right through, so that the wound it causes will never close into a scar.
Their liver grows at the full moon, as Isidore says, just as certain sea creatures grow, like shellfish, which likewise shrink again as the moon wanes.
The onager is the wild ass. On the fifteenth day of March, as Isidore says, it brays twelve times at night and as many times during the day; from this it is known that the equinox has occurred.

When males are born, the fathers, as Solinus says, hide them and bite off their testicles; the mothers, wary of this, give birth in secret and hide the young. Female onagers delight in abundance of lust and, not keeping to the proper measure of decency, often become hateful to the males because of this. And we see the same among men: wives held in hatred by their husbands when they are moved too impatiently toward lechery. The onager, by natural cunning, releases its dung when pursued by dogs, since it is fragrant to dogs; by holding them back with this it deceives the dogs and so escapes. A male onager without a female, when the mating season comes, climbs the mountain heights and, burning with desire for lust, draws in the wind through its nostrils and brays violently, so that it shakes the other animals with the terror of its braying.
[on onagers]

The 'onocentaur,' as [Isidore] says, is a monstrous animal, of double nature, having a head like that of an ass and a body like that of a man. Others hold that it is half man and half ass: from the navel up a man, below it an ass.

The sheep is a well-known animal. Shepherds take a sign from those sheep that can endure the winter: they throw icy water over the animal's tail. The sheep that shakes it off is strong; one that does not shake it off is weak. Lack of understanding abounds more in sheep than in other quadrupeds. A sick sheep readily infects others, and for this reason must be separated from the rest. It is natural for the ram to disdain the lambs and favor the more grown sheep. Its ferocity is restrained by its own horn. Thunder brings on miscarriage in solitary sheep; the remedy against thunder is to gather them into a flock. Sheep fatten by drinking much water, and more so in the afternoon, if the water they drink is muddy. Hence some shepherds give them salt in their feed, so that they drink more and give more milk. Aristotle: sheep become sterile from fatness. The milk of black sheep is more abundant and better, but with goats it is the reverse.

Ambrose: a sheep grazes insatiably on grass, because it senses that a harsh winter is coming, so as to fill itself with fodder before all the grass fails under the burning frost. Sheep pastured in dry places live longer; if they graze often in marshy places, they cannot live long. A sheep can scarcely be driven from a burning house, and if it is driven out, unless held back by force, it runs back to the fire. If young sheep rush eagerly to mate, this is a very bad sign, for it foretells plague among them.

Aristotle: if sheep drink salt water, they will mate earlier. If sheep conceive facing the north wind, they bear males; if facing the south wind, females. If the veins under a sheep's tongue are white, it will bear a white lamb; if black, a black one; if red, a red one; if of two colors, one of two colors. The same: sheep die when they become too fat in the kidneys. A sheep fattens on clear water. The same: grazing helps sheep at the end of the day, and movement too.
Michael Scot: lamb's flesh is very good and wholesome for the strong and healthy, and unwholesome for the sick.

Isidore: the lamb ['agnus'] is so called from 'recognizing' ['agnoscendo'], because more than other animals it knows its mother — even in a large flock it recognizes its mother's bleating — or from 'agnon,' which means 'pious.'
Aristotle: the wool of sheep eaten by a wolf takes in more lice when woven.
Alexander: good parchment is never made from the hide of a sheep that died of disease, nor from a thick hide.
Note that it is said: powdered centaury mixed with salt is good for sheep against swallows; likewise poppy husk prepared the same way.
Panthers, as Jacques says, are beasts akin in kind to leopards, distinguished by their spotted markings.

Solinus: in Africa, because of the scarcity of water, various wild beasts gather at the rivers, where lionesses mate with different beasts, whether by force or by desire, and from this union panthers are said to be born. The panther is fierce and very sharp in attack, and its body's variegated coloring matches its temperament.

The panther, as Solinus says, is an animal of varied color, exceedingly beautiful, marked over with small round spots, so that its eyes gleam amid tawny rings, shading into blue or white. This animal, however, is very gentle, and has only the dragon as its enemy.

When it has eaten and is satisfied with various foods, it hides itself in its den, as the Physiologus says, and sleeps. Rising from sleep after three days, it lets out a roar; the other beasts, hearing this, gather and follow the sweetness of the scent that issues from its mouth, though they are frightened by the harshness of its face. For this reason, keeping its face hidden, it seizes those it has lured with its remaining sweetness.
This beast, as Isidore says, gives birth only once. For the young, not waiting for the proper hour, tear at the womb with their claws, leaving the mother thereby half-dead and unable to bear again.
For, as Pliny says, animals with sharp claws often cannot give birth safely, since they are injured inwardly by their moving young.
The 'pilosus' is an animal, as the Gloss on Isaiah says, which has the shape of a man above, but below ends in the feet of a beast.

Jerome describes this beast in the Life of Paul the Hermit, saying that above it is a man with a rough forehead bearing horns, and below it ends in the feet of a goat; such creatures are called satyrs, or fauns, or incubi.

The polecat, as the Book of Nature says, gets its name from its stench, since it smells foul, especially when angered. On its left side, like the badger, it has shorter legs than on the right. It is most greedy for hens and their eggs. It lives only on flesh and the like, and dwells in the high, hidden parts of buildings.

The 'pirolus,' as the Book of Nature says, is a small beast, larger but not longer than the weasel, reddish in body and white on the belly; it has a bushy tail nearly as big as itself. When it needs to cross water while moving to a new region for food, it gathers a very light piece of wood upon the water, and, sitting upon it, raises its tail aloft like a ship's sail, and, with the wind blowing, crosses using its tail.

The ape, as Isidore says, is a beast thickly covered with hair, with limbs nearly identical to man's in almost every respect. It is sensitive to the elements, and rejoices at the new moon, but grieves during the moon's middle and hollow phases.
Solinus: apes are keener in taste than other animals. They are restless in gesture, fierce in biting; they are never so tame that they are not liable to turn savage.

As the Experimentator says, it strongly desires to be adorned, hence it puts on gloves and shoes set as traps for it, when it is meant to be caught. It recognizes its master returning after the passage of many years. It gladly plays with children, and, given the chance, strangles them. It gladly eats apples and nuts, but when it finds a bitter rind on them, throws away the rind together with the nut, refusing the sweet because of the bitter. Whoever harms it, it holds a grudge against; it has a special affection for its young. The young that tame apes bear within houses they show to everyone and delight in being handled.

Although apes are, in outward appearance, nearly similar to men, inwardly, however, they have no such structure or arrangement in common with men — indeed, as Aristotle says, less so than some other animals. It lacks what a human body has, since it has no navel. The female ape's vulva is like a woman's, and the male's member like a dog's.

The bull, as the Book of Nature says, is an animal robust in strength and, among sociable beasts, gentle enough, except toward those that oppose the rest by their rapacity, whom it opposes in turn. In fighting they use their tongues out, doing nothing with their teeth, for they have no fear in their teeth. When they graze on grass, they do not harm the roots, but take only what is on the surface. The older bulls are, the more tender their flesh, if they are well fattened. All females have a finer and sharper voice than the males, except in the kind of cows, in which it is the reverse.

Yoked oxen, as Isidore says, show a remarkable devotion to their companions; each seeks out the one with whom it is used to drawing the plow, and by frequent lowing shows its affectionate concern if that companion is missing. By frequent washing with warm water they are made to grow fat. The ox has stronger and tougher heart-sinews than other animals, but the bull has even stronger ones still. Beef produces coarse, turbid, and melancholic blood, and is digested slowly unless taken with strong wine and garlic. If you wish to breed males, the Greeks say the bull's left testicle should be bound during mating; for females, the right.

Alexander: cattle know to keep to their stall when rain threatens. When excess overtakes a bull, it dies suddenly and does not suffer a long illness. We see the same among country folk, who, unused to luxury and accustomed to daily toil, likewise die quickly. A cow's horns are harder than the male's.

As the great Basil says, drinking a bull's blood is deadly. The warm blood of a bull, applied as a fomentation, helps set broken bones. The gall of oxen mixed with honey draws out a thorn, splinter of wood, or piece of iron.
Philosophus: a wild bull tethered to a fig tree becomes tame.

The 'tragelaphus' is an animal forbidden by the Law. As Isidore says, it has the appearance of a stag in many respects, having shaggy shoulders like a he-goat and a bearded chin like a he-goat's. Its head bristles with branching horns, powerful enough by their strength and as weapons to drive off any adversary and keep itself safe from enemies.
The mole, as the Book of Nature says, is a small, black, and blind animal.
This creature, as the Gloss says, is born from earth made wet and muddy, but corrupted. Fittingly, it dwells in the earth and lives on a diet of worms.

A mole, burnt to powder and sprinkled with egg white, is a remedy applied to the face against leprosy. The blood of a mole, freshly killed, smeared on a head stripped bare of hair, is said to make the hair grow back.

The tiger is a beast marked with varied spots, remarkable in strength and speed, and the river Tigris takes its name from it. Hyrcania breeds these. They are most savage and of incomparable fury, especially when, robbed of its cubs, it pursues hunters, who could scarcely escape unless they threw glass shields and glass globes in its path. Once the tiger examines these, seeing itself as though in a mirror and thinking it has found its own offspring, it stops, kissing and embracing the glass, and finally, trampling it underfoot, finds nothing there. Meanwhile the hunters flee away.
Aristotle: it is in many ways similar to a bull, inclining somewhat toward a reddish color. Its flesh is sweet, which is also why it is hunted.

The unicorn is a small animal, as Isidore says, considering the strength of its body. It has short legs, but for its size it is exceedingly fierce, so much so that it can be overcome by force by no hunter.

But Isidore and Jacques say: it is captured by leaving a virgin girl alone in the forest. Approaching her, having set aside all its ferocity, it reveres the girl's chaste purity, and, laying its head in the girl's lap, falls asleep there, and is captured by hunters and displayed as a spectacle in a royal palace. This animal signifies Christ, who before the Incarnation raged in heaven, punishing the angels for their pride, on earth punishing men for Adam's disobedience, for lust like the Sodomites, for gluttony like the children of Israel. Him the glorious Virgin Mary captured in the wilderness of this world, when, drawn by the bosom of her wondrous chastity, he entered her womb, and at last, killed by the Jews as by most cruel hunters, and rising again from that death, he was placed at his Father's right hand, as in a king's palace, to be beheld by all the saints in his Ascension.

The bear is an exceedingly fierce animal, misshapen in its limbs, skinned it would nearly resemble a man's limbs. Its greatest strength is in its forelegs and loins, but its head is weak. Ambrose: the she-bear, on the thirtieth day, bears young a little larger than mice, and unformed.

As Pliny says, she licks the shapeless flesh she has produced and, by tending and shaping it, brings it into proper form. In the offspring itself, as it is born, no limb is visible except the marks of the claws. Pliny: bears mate as humans do.

Solinus: males respect pregnant she-bears in seclusion. Nothing is rarer than to see a she-bear giving birth. Female bears are stronger and bolder than males, as is also the case with leopards; they are quickly tamed and are more cunning.

For medicinal purposes the bear eats ants and crabs; cooked bear meat, remarkably, is said to increase in size, as Pliny says, which is contrary to the nature of all other meats. The bear is so pestilential that no wild creature touches what its breath has touched, and things it has breathed upon rot more quickly. When a bear is captured, it is blinded this way: a red-hot iron is shown to it, and it at once loses its sight. It can scarcely stand still. A bear nearly always keeps growing.

Solinus: the bear lies in wait for beehives, for they crave honeycombs above all, and nothing draws them more eagerly than honey. Hunters therefore dig a pit meant to catch the bear, into which they want it to fall so that, once trapped there, it may be killed, and they smear the path toward the pit with honey, so that the bear, following the honeyed trail and licking as it goes, eventually falls into the pit.
The fox, when the danger of death draws near, as Ambrose says, seeks out the pine tree and takes as food the tear or sap that flows from the pine, and so recovers its health and prolongs its life.

The Experimentator says that foxes do not labor at digging their own dens, but a certain beast we call the badger does. For when the badger has dug a burrow to rest in, the cunning fox burdens the entrance of the burrow with its own dung, so that, the burrow fouled by the stench of the rotten waste, it becomes worthless, since the badger abhors the stench and abandons the place, and so the cunning beast takes possession of the spot. The Experimentator says the fox has foul breath, and is also foul from behind. It preys chiefly on domestic animals. If fox flesh is burned, its ash, taken with wine, is good for asthmatics. The blood of its fat is of great benefit for earache. If a fox eats almonds, it is said to die. It suffers a heating of the liver in summer. This creature also, when hungry and finding nothing to eat, feigns death and lies on its back, drawing breath with its tongue hanging out. Then birds, carelessly swooping down as if to a carcass, are seized in its open mouth and devoured.

The fox, according to Isidore, is called as if 'volupes,' being nimble of foot and never moving in a straight path, but a winding one. It sometimes escapes dogs by pretending to be a dog among dogs with a similar bark, and by hanging itself from a branch it makes the dogs lose the trail. Caught in a snare, it sometimes bites off its own foot, so as to escape even by this means. When no escape at all remains open, it feigns death, so as to break free from the snare and flee once released. It also sometimes feigns death for the sake of food, and so seizes and devours the birds that come down to the carcass.

A bird of good wing, that is, swift in flight, has weak, that is feeble, feet, as the swallow and the like. Small-bodied birds sing more than large-bodied ones, and this especially at mating time. Every bird with a curved talon has good flight, and every bird with a spur on its leg, like the cock, has poor and weak flight. Every bird with clawed toes lives on flesh; others feed on fruit, worms, and reptiles. Every bird with (separated) toes on its feet eats flesh. Every bird of prey hunts prey of a different kind than its own, and in this birds differ from fish. The sparrowhawk alone lacks this restraint. The flesh of flesh-eating birds is tastier than other flesh, unless something in their particular nature specially works against it. All young birds, while small, have long bellies and navels, which shorten as they grow. Birds do not descend on a foul-smelling carcass unless it has a good flavor. Generally the males of birds live longer than the females, and the reason is that females are more often weakened to the point of death by brooding. No bird has a bladder, because of the scarcity of what it drinks, but chiefly because the excess of water passes, in all birds, into their feathers. Every bird with long legs has a long neck; with short legs, a short neck — except birds that have skin between their toes, like the goose. There is greater fecundity in small birds than in large ones. They say eggs have such power that wood soaked in egg will not burn, nor will cloth be scorched near it; mixed with lime, egg is also said to glue together broken pieces of glass. Isidore says these two things, though they are much doubted among us. Birds that lay many eggs do so in the most hidden way. The larger the animal, the longer it is formed in the womb.

Aristotle: flesh-eating birds lay eggs only once a year, except swallows, which lay twice. The same: sickness in birds is recognized from the disorder of their wings. The same: when birds fight one another, they apply wild marjoram to their wounds. The same: birds of prey are bilious and thus very hot. The same: all hook-taloned birds, when they see their young flying behind them, strike them and drive them from the nest, and once the young are fully fledged the parents show no more concern for them, except the crow, which cares for its young for a long time. The same: for the most part hook-taloned birds lay few eggs. The same: long, sharp-pointed eggs produce males; round eggs, and those round even at the pointed end, produce females. The young form, however, at the pointed end. The same: eggs have two colors. The beginning of generation is from the white, nourishment from the yolk. The same: eggs can only be fertile if conceived by mating with a male and penetrated by his spirit. The same: the chick is fully formed in ten days, apart from the time of its actual generation. From the egg, the broad end emerges first, then the pointed end. Every kind of bird is born twice: first the eggs are laid, and then they are shaped and given life by the heat of the mother's body. The same: thunder spoils eggs during incubation. The same: egg white dropped into a thick liquid like syrup thins and refines it.

The eagle, as Augustine says, is the noblest of birds, as befits the queen of birds. It is a great predator and lives on flesh. Its eyesight is so sharp that it can gaze on the sun's rays with an unflinching stare; hence it gladly sits turned toward the sun. It holds its young up by their talons against the sun's rays. Those it sees hold their gaze unmoving, it keeps and feeds as worthy of its kind; but any it finds turning their eyes away, it casts out as unworthy of its lineage.

The eagle, as Adelinus says, when weighed down by old age, notes a very cold spring and, flying up high directly above it, rises past all the clouds. From the heat of the nearby sun, the film over its eyes is burned away, and then, descending suddenly with the heat still upon it, it plunges into the coldest water three times, and rising from this at once seeks its nest, and among its young, now strong enough to hunt, seized as though by a kind of fever from the unevenness of cold and heat, it sheds its feathers in a sweat, and is warmed and fed by its own young, until, recovering its plumage and feathers, it is made new again.

Augustine: its beak, too, when the hook of it grows so excessively that it can scarcely take food even with effort, it dashes against a rock in a natural way, and by this dashing the hook is broken off and restored to fitness for feeding. The young of eagles are without cry or complaint.

Jacques: it keeps an 'aetites' stone in its nest — or, as some hold, a jet stone — useful for many remedies. This stone, as though pregnant, has a small stone inside it that can be heard rattling within like an unborn child. It is said to keep this stone in its nest against the excessive heat that is natural to the eagle, lest its eggs perish, cooked by too much heat; for the heat of fire cannot harm the 'aetites' stone.

Others also say, as the Experimentator reports, that they place two precious stones called 'indes' in their nest, without whose presence the eagle cannot give birth. The eagle shares its prey with other birds and lets them eat with it. But let them beware: if the food set before it does not suffice, it seizes and eats one of the birds eating with it. The crow sometimes follows the eagle, and when the eagle has for a long time pretended not to notice, it finally seizes the crow with its talons.

The feathers of eagles, as Pliny says, when mixed with the feathers of other birds, seem by a kind of natural instinct to resent them and, unable to bear them, consume them. The eagle's right foot is larger than its left; it carries its young on its shoulders, so as to encourage them to fly. All noble birds, on seeing an eagle, are struck with fear and lose their boldness that day, nor can they easily fly out after prey.
The Gloss says the gyrfalcon captures the eagle.
Alexander: the eagle, it is said, by its imperious cry alone checks the movement of other birds.
A long fast is compensated by taking in a great quantity of food; it 'diligently urges its young to fly.'

As Gamaliel says, when it fears the ambush of archers, it carries off its young perched on its back, and interposes its own body between them and the archer like a shield, so as to take the blow itself if need be. When there is a deadly plague among the flocks, it is said that eating a single carcass is, remarkably, the cause of that very plague.

The harpy is a bird, as Adelinus says, dwelling in remote parts of the world, in a wilderness place called the Strophades near the Ionian Sea. It is almost always insatiably, ravenously hungry. It has hooked talons, always ready for tearing and seizing. This creature has only a human face, but nothing of human virtue in it; for it rages with a ferocity beyond human measure. It is said to kill the first man it sees in the wilderness.
