Then, when it happens upon water and beholds its own face in it, seeing at once that it has killed one like itself, it grieves beyond measure, sometimes even unto death, and laments for the whole rest of its life. This bird, when sometimes tamed, speaks, taught to imitate a human voice, but it lacks reason.

The heron, as Jacques, Isidore, and Ambrose say, is a bird named as though 'ardua' [lofty], because of its high flights. For it dreads rainstorms and for this reason flies above the clouds, so as not to feel the violence of the whirling storms. So then, by flying higher, it escapes the tempest. This bird, though it seeks its food in the water, nonetheless builds its nest in forests and in tall trees. For hawks are hostile to it. But the heron turns its rear toward the hawk and casts out its droppings, at whose touch the hawk's feathers rot. It has a single intestine, like the stork.

Geese, as the cock does, announce the hours of the night by squawking. They are also said to reveal thieves by their squawking, and this because, as Isidore says, no animal senses the smell of a man so quickly.
Sometimes they lay without mating, but such eggs are without young, as Aristotle says.

And the Experimentator says: while their young are not yet strong, one goose always keeps watch with neck erect, so that no eagle comes from above. It distinguishes between an eagle and a vulture, which indeed is difficult for a man to do. Of these, the wild ones direct their flights according to the blowing of the winds, whether south or north. When the north wind blows, they seek shelter. Except for the sake of feeding, they scarcely ever rest from flight; so delightful is flying to them that they rarely sleep. But for domestic geese, flight is a burden; grazing is their chief business, resting and sleeping their special delight.

The duck is a well-known bird, whose young, as soon as they leave the egg, are so vigorous that, even if the mother happens to die or be taken away, they live without a nurse. When many males are together, they are driven by such a madness of lust that, competing with one another to mate with a single female duck, they kill her.

The hawk, as the Book of Nature says, is a noble bird, considerably larger but much slower than the falcon, though more cautious in guarding itself, for it is more measured in flight. Once it has caught a bird, it pierces or digs at its side with its beak, so as to feed only on the heart. Hence its master, the falconer, rewards the victor only with the heart, and keeps the rest for his own use. The hawk, once stripped of its old feathers, spreads its wings toward the south, so as to grow new ones, and this so that the pores open to the sun's heat and new feathers grow back more readily. For nature is, in almost all the things of the world that die and are born, a teacher of usefulness. When it is healthy, it holds its feathers erect; when sick, drooping.
It is carried on the hand, as the Experimentator says, so that it may fly toward the right hand to receive something.

This bird drives its tender young toward prey by striking them with its wings, and casts them out of the nest without bringing them food, so that they do not grow lazy once grown, according to Ambrose. Small wonder, if creatures accustomed to seizing find it distasteful to nurture.
A hawk boiled in oil of roses, as Pliny says, is a most effective remedy for ailments of the limbs.

Alexander: in winter the hawk holds under its feet through the whole night the bird it has caught before nightfall, but, come sunrise, lets it fly free even while hungry, and, if it should later meet that same bird again while hunting, does not pursue it. It changes the color of its eyes and its beak.
Augustine: [something] kills the hawk.

The 'amraham' is a bird of the East, as Aristotle says, which nests on mountains where man cannot climb, and so its nest is never found, and its young are very rarely seen either; for its young do not come down to lower ground unless they are entirely strong and fully like their mother. Apply this against hypocrites.

The 'anchatis' is a bird, as Pliny says; it is nourished on a diet of grass, and for this reason has a hatred for horses. Wherever it sees them come upon it while grazing, it flees and takes vengeance as it can, mocking the horses' whinnying by imitating their own whinnies back at them in mockery. Though small in body, this bird is nonetheless fertile, for it bears twelve young at once.

The lark, as the Book of Nature says, is a bird named from 'praise' ['laus'], because with the greatest delight, wings spread in the air, it rejoices in the fine weather with the modulation of its voice.

Pliny calls this the 'crested lark'; for under a clouded or rainy sky it scarcely or never sings. It heralds the coming of day at dawn with the joy of its voice; sitting on the ground it scarcely or never sings.
It sings while ascending, as the Experimentator says; it climbs little by little, but descends suddenly, like a falling stone.

Philosophus: it fears the hawk so much that, when attacked by one, it flies into a man's bosom or offers itself, crouched to the ground, to be taken by his hand, well aware that a man is more likely to pity it than the hawk — and rightly so, since the one sometimes shows mercy, the other never.

Kingfishers are small birds, as Pliny says. This bird, the kingfisher, lays its eggs on the sand in wintertime, and this precisely when the sea rises most and the shore is struck most violently by the waves, so that the grace of this bird might shine forth all the more through the sudden solemn calm that follows. For wherever the sea is stormy, once the eggs are laid it quickly grows gentle, and every storm subsides, and the sea becomes calm to the winds, for as long as the kingfisher broods over her eggs. For this bird dwells at sea. The eggs take seven days to hatch, after which she brings out her young. She adds another seven days besides, during which she rears her brood, until they begin to grow up. So great is the grace this tiniest of birds has from God, that sailors count on the calm of these fourteen days, which they also call the 'halcyon days,' during which no stir of stormy weather is feared. This bird signifies those who, in a time of prosperity, confess themselves to be idle and as though fruitless, but when they see adversity rise up against them, only then do they trust that they possess the fruit of their rewards. Hence it is said that 'the apostles went rejoicing,' and so on. By their merits it sometimes happens that the hoped-for fruits are not withheld from their deserts, and that times of peace are granted by the merciful Lord, who indeed does not allow us to be tempted beyond what we can bear.

The owl gets its name from the sound of its cry. Other birds are caught by means of this bird, and it signifies the sinner who sins openly and scandalously. The owl, as the Experimentator says, drinks the eggs of the dove, hunts mice, dwells in churches, drinks the oil from lamps, and yet fouls them with its droppings. When attacked by other birds that live in the light, it defends itself lying on its back with the talons of its feet. If an owl's heart is placed on the left side of a sleeping woman, she will tell everything she has done. Whoever anoints clouded eyes with it clears them. These birds represent, within the Church, insolent and dissolute clerics who, though they live off the rich benefices of the Church, nonetheless stain her with their sins, and, when reproved by good men, attack them with the cruelty of their claws. It is indeed a bird laden with feathers, but always held down by heavy sloth.

The caladrius, as Jacques and Isidore say, is a wholly white bird. The inner part of its thigh removes clouding from the eyes. For the nature of the caladrius is such that, if it is brought several times to a sick man, it gives those standing by a sure sign of whether the sick man will die or live. For if it turns its face away from the sick man and averts its eyes, it is a sign of death. But if it does not avert its eyes, it is a sign of life. For then it fixes its gaze on his face and draws all the sicknesses of that sick man into itself, and flies up into the air; there it burns up the sicknesses and scatters them, and at once the sick man is healed. Kings in ancient times used to keep these birds enclosed in royal courtyards. Alexander is said to have found these birds in Persia. The caladrius has one thick bone in its leg, whose marrow, if someone anoints clouded eyes with it, clears them.

The swan is a bird named from 'singing,' because it pours forth the sweetness of song in measured tones. Jacques: the swan has white feathers but black flesh. By nature it foretells its own death in a song of joy and rejoicing as it is about to die; its strength lies in its wings. When death draws near, it fixes a feather in its brain, and so sings sweetly. It is of bilious complexion and therefore prone to anger. It swims with one foot while steering itself like a sail with the other. It eats little in proportion to the size of its body; it has very fierce teeth-like edges in its beak, with which it cuts up its food. Struck on the head it dies easily, though it can withstand many other injuries.
The 'caristae,' as Solinus says, are birds that fly into flames unharmed, so that neither their feathers nor their flesh are in any way consumed by the fire.

Storks, as Isidore says, are birds of ash-grey color; they are so called, as Solinus says, from the sound they make by clattering, which is more a matter of the beak than of the voice. They clatter for three reasons: for the arrival of a mate — and this in joy; for birds flying overhead — and this in fear; and for anger — and this in self-defense. When they cross the sea, crows lead the way before their flock as guides. They have the greatest care and affection for their young, so much so that, in tending their nests so devotedly and sitting in constant brooding, they shed their own feathers. But the young show no less remarkable devotion to their mothers; for as long a time as the mothers spend rearing their young, so long a time are the mothers in turn cared for by their young — hence it is also called the 'pious bird.'

This kind of bird lies in wait for serpents in many ways, and, although it eats them and other venomous creatures, it nonetheless does not die from this, as Adelinus says. It eats toads, however, only when very hungry, and in this the toad's natural repulsiveness is noted.
The stork's stomach is a remedy against poisons, as Pliny says. In Asia there is a plain where they gather and clamor together, and tear apart whichever of them arrives last, and then depart.

The calandra lark is a small bird, quite similar to the [common] lark. It delights its hearers with a remarkable modulation of voice; hence it happens that it is caught by men and kept shut up in cages. But, forgetful of its captivity and misfortune, it scarcely lets a single hour of the day pass without song; indeed it seems to count it a delight to be a captive in this way, so undistracted is it by anything else. It is not anxious even about food or about this present life, but rejoices in the one thing needful to it: to range freely through song and to practice, every hour, the diverse voices of birds. For it imitates the voices of all birds, and in this is spiritually signified the joy of contemplatives, who, even in this present life, being scarcely or rarely mindful of their exile because of the sweetness of God, seem, according to the Apostle, already to have their citizenship in the heavens.
The raven, as Isidore says, is a bird whose female broods the eggs while the male brings her food.

The raven, as Augustine says, does not feed its hatched young until it sees, by examining them, that their feathers have turned black. Hence they are said to go seven days without any nourishment at all; on the seventh day, however, they turn black. Ravens sometimes cast some of their young out of the nest, wearied of feeding them. They are said to conceive and give birth through the mouth.

John: eggs pass out through a raven's mouth and through its lower parts as well. Ravens are said to become pregnant if they happen to eat a raven's egg. The raven is noisy and forms various sounds, namely sixty-four of them.

As Fulgentius says, they sometimes mate while flying. The raven eats the owl's eggs by day, and the owl the raven's eggs by night; the raven is stronger by day, the owl by night. There is a certain kind of raven in the East that fights with the donkey and the bull. As these flee, the raven flies above them and dashes itself violently against their eyes, and so, blinding them, renders them useless to their owners, and consequently, once killed and skinned, their carcasses become food for birds — and so this wicked bird overcomes strong animals, just as a wicked woman overcomes strong men. The raven by nature loves the fox, and so helps it against the bird called the 'achylon.' The 'achylon,' however, is the raven's enemy.
Crows, as Pliny says, are of the same kind [as ravens]; they are also seized by sickness at the solstice.

As the Experimentator says, noble birds attack them as though they were their enemies, and often to their own harm. For when noble birds have long endured their persistent attacks, at last, overcome by impatience, they tear the troublesome creatures apart. The crow gladly feeds on nuts, and when it sometimes cannot break the hardness of a nut with its beak, it flies up high and drops it once among the rocks, and again, and repeatedly, until, cracked, it can be broken open. The male feeds the crow while she broods.

The cuckoo does not vary its call in singing, but always repeats the same note. It is a most lazy bird and unsettled in its dwelling. It lays its eggs in the nest of some other small bird of a different kind, and removes from the number of eggs it finds there, so that, presumably, the little bird will not find too many eggs and reject them as not her own. The deceived little bird thus broods the foreign egg placed among her own and hatches the young, nor is she clever enough to distinguish the offspring by size, since it is smaller in shape than her own young. And so, as Pliny says, the cuckoo, while still sitting weak among the rest of the brood in the nest, nevertheless snatches food from the other young with a natural greed, and grows fat from this surfeit ahead of the rest, and becomes sleeker. Charmed by its handsome appearance, the foster-mother rejoices in its form and marvels at herself for having produced such a creature, and condemns all her own young by comparison to it, and lets it consume her out of sheer admiration. And this is its reward to her: not knowing its own ignorance, it finds ignorance rewarded. For once the mistaken mother has raised the cuckoo and nourished it to the strength needed for flight, the cuckoo turns instead upon its foster-mother and kills her as she pursues it. The cuckoo is said to be stripped of its feathery garment in winter. It enters either a hole in the earth or the hollow of trees, and so in summer gathers what it will feed on in winter.

Isidore reports of the cuckoo something quite doubtful: he says that, when the time comes for them to migrate, they cling, taken up onto the shoulders of kites, because of their own short and feeble flight, so that they do not grow exhausted and fail over the long stretches of open air. Their saliva is said to generate cicadas.

The 'coredulus' is a bird, as Isidore says, named as though 'heart-eating'; for, living on flesh and prey, it especially longs to be sated on the heart, signifying assuredly God himself, who says: 'give me, my son, your heart.'
On which Augustine says: for he paid so great a price that he alone ought to possess it.
The dove, as Augustine says, is a gentle bird.
It does not tear with its beak, and it has no gall, as Bede says.
Aristotle, however, says that it does have gall, but not in the place where other animals have it; for it has it in the intestine.

Bede's apparent contradiction is thus resolved, when he says it has no gall, this being understood as: in the place where other animals have it. It rouses love with a kiss, walks in flocks, harms no one, does not live on carrion, feeds on pure grain, has moaning in place of song, and rears others' young. The dove recovers its sight nine times over, and nests high up, as Jacques and Bede say, where no evil beast can reach. Let your own way of life, then, be in the heavens. It rests more gladly over water, both to quench its thirst and to see in the water the shadow of an approaching hawk.

There is a certain tree of the East, as Isidore says, called in Greek 'paradixion,' which in Latin means 'facing the right hand.' The fruit of this tree is sweet, and doves take wondrous delight in it, sheltering under its shade and branches. In those same regions there is also a certain kind of dragon that lies in wait for these very doves; but the dragon by nature dreads that tree so much that it fears even to come near its shadow. So then, while the doves sit in the tree, the dragon lies in wait far off and watches to see if any of them leaves the tree and becomes its prey. But if the shadow falls on the left side, the dragon attacks from the right, and if on the right, from the left. Understand the dragons as demons, the doves as faithful souls, the 'paradixion' as the cross of Christ, at whose right hand is his mother, and the shadow of the tree as the sign of the cross.
Aristotle: doves are of the greatest chastity and know no adultery.

They do not break faith, as Pliny says, and love their shared home, and unless one is single, chaste, or widowed, it does not leave the home. They always bear two young, first a male, and after three days a female. Both sit in turn: the female broods from noon until morning, the male the rest of the time; the young hatch on the eighteenth day. When doves find a stray dove, they gather it in with themselves. And they eat small stones to aid the temperance of their stomach, being of a very hot nature. They fight with wings raised; their dung is extremely fiery, which they cast out of the nest and teach their young to cast out too. The blood of a dove, a swallow, and a turtledove, taken from beneath the right wing and applied to the eye, heals it, for it is sharp and has a dissolving power. The male casts his grown young out of the nest, but before casting them out, mates with the female again out of concern for a new brood. The dove suffers greatly in laying its eggs; and if she is slow to lay, she is struck bitterly [by the male]. It is proper to doves to drink for a long time; for they do not lift their heads while drinking until they have had enough. The young of doves are better and healthier in spring and autumn than at other times, and this because then they live chiefly on grain. Pliny: the fresh flesh of the dove and the swallow, tied together, are good against snakebite. It is certain that some doves never know a male, while others remain widowed once they have lost their first mate. Such doves avoid the common home of those doves that are paired in mating, so as not to be troubled by the disturbances of the males, and they flee and dwell instead among the rocks. The sparrowhawk lies in wait for doves especially when they have been preening their feathers with their beaks. For they take great care over this; they gaze admiringly at their own beauty, and it is then that they are caught.

The quail, as the Book of Nature says, is a bird we commonly call 'quascula,' but which the Greeks call 'ortygia,' because such birds were first seen on the island of Ortygia. It is called 'ortygometra,' as though 'leading the flock.' They gather to cross the sea and, falling by night onto ships in great numbers, sometimes sink them under their sails.

Solinus: they have set times for their arrival; when summer is over they cross the sea, and, drawing near land, that is to a harbor, are seized upon by watching hawks; hence it is necessary for all of them to press a leader of another kind into service, through whom they escape the first dangers, for they take crows as their guides. Be mindful, then, that it was said to the devil: 'you will lie in wait for his heel,' that is, his end; for it is then that we are most gravely tempted. So then, urge on your guides, the angels, to protect you from the attack of the hellish hawk. Among quail, females are the rarest of all birds, just as among fish scallops are the rarest. Among the human race, however, fewer and rarer males are born than females, and the reason is this: human nature, prone to mating at indiscriminate times, mates with women more often in the evening and in the first hours of the night, precisely when their bodies are still filled with the vapors of food and their spirits not yet purified by sleep. If offspring is conceived then, it takes on the weaker sex, that is, the female. But those conceived at dawn, when it is the hour of the blood and the body and spirits have been purified by the evaporation of the vapors, more often obtain the male sex at their conception. This bird alone, among all the living creatures of the earth, suffers the falling sickness along with man. It has very coarse food and certain poisonous seeds, for which reasons the tables of the wise have condemned them.

The goldfinch is a small bird, taking its name, as Isidore says, from the fact that it feeds on thistles ['cardones' or 'carduus'], and it seems remarkable that this little bird should be nourished by the sharp spines of thistles. This bird is adorned with black and yellow on its body and red coloring on its head. It is commonly said of this bird that, shut up in a cage, it draws up water placed below it, by thread, in a little vessel suspended, to itself with its beak, and, its foot sometimes placed on the thread as well, once it touches the little vessel it quenches its thirst by drinking — and this indeed is a marvel of nature, which gave such cunning to the small goldfinch, a cunning nature was unwilling to grant to the ox or the ass or to large animals.

The 'crochilos,' as Pliny says, is a bird we call in Italy the king of birds. It is indeed the smallest of all birds, but, as Pliny says, the smaller its body, the greater its speed. It has such boldness that it dares to make attempts even against the eagle, the queen of birds. In winter many crochili gather together in a single cave, so that the heat, which is small in such tiny bodies, may be increased to a proper warmth by the crowd's contribution.
It is said in Ecclesiastes: 'two shall keep each other warm; how shall one alone be warmed?'

The Diomedean birds are so named, as Solinus says, after King Diomedes; the Greeks call them 'erodii.' They are the size of swans, of a white color, with fiery eyes and toothed beaks, and they fly in flocks. The first in the order leads the flock, and the last drives it on. When they grieve with tearful cries, they signal either a coming change or the death of their king. They leave their nests toward the east to feed; the entrance of the nest, facing west, receives them on their return. Solinus and Jacques: if a Greek approaches them, they are said to be gentle toward him, but they attack other peoples with bites.

The 'erodius,' also called the 'griffalle,' as the Gloss on Leviticus says, in the passage where unclean birds are forbidden, or the gyrfalcon as the Book of Nature calls it, is the noblest of all birds. It is of a sky-blue color, though most of its body inclines toward white except on the breast. This bird is so strong and large, as the Gloss on Leviticus says, that it overcomes and captures the eagle itself, though the eagle is the strongest of birds. In flying at its prey it draws its feet up to its breast and so strikes the prey. If it does not catch its prey on the first stoop, it climbs high up again, and, out of indignation, scarcely returns to the lure. When it sees its prey, it rouses itself with a shake and, if it is fit to be taken, singles it out.

The phoenix is a bird of Arabia, as Solinus, Jacques, Isidore, and Ambrose say, without equal in the world, living alone for a span of three hundred and forty years. It is the size of an eagle, with a head as noble as a peacock's, a crested throat, golden splendor about its neck, and purple toward its rear parts; its tail is sky-blue, into which rose-colored feathers are worked with wondrous variety. And when, weighed down with the burden of advancing age, it begins to grow heavy, it builds itself, in the loftiest parts of the East, in a most beautiful tree set above a most pleasant spring, an altar as though it were a nest, out of frankincense and myrrh and cinnamon and precious spices. Then, by beating its wings, it draws the burning orbs of the sun into itself, rushes upon the pile it has built, and, the spices set ablaze by the sun's heat, it is itself equally consumed and burned. Then, after a few days of its own burning, a worm born from the very ashes of the phoenix, within a short time, puts on the flight-feathers of wings, and then is most perfectly re-formed into its original bird shape. Isidore says that the phoenix entered the Egyptian city of Heliopolis, in the month of Adar, that is, April, and, its wings laden with various spices, mounted a pile of firewood that had been laid out for sacrifice by a priest of the Lord, and burned itself upon the pile amid the spices it had carried on its wings. On the first day after the day of its burning, the priest, coming, found the wood he had placed on the altar burnt, and, searching the ashes, found a small worm giving off the sweetest fragrance. On the second day, the little worm was found already formed into a bird.

On the third day, however, in its own whole and most perfect state, bidding the priest farewell, it flew away. In this city, as Haymo says, before the coming of the Savior, a temple was built in the manner of the temple of Jerusalem, in honor of the most high God, by Onias, son of Onias, by order of Ptolemy, king of Egypt, according to the word: 'there shall be an altar of the Lord in the land of Egypt.' In this city, as Haymo says, the blessed Virgin Mary, fleeing from Herod with her son, often dwelt. This bird signifies the holy soul, which has the greatness of the eagle as regards contemplation, and the beauty of the peacock's head as regards purity of mind. In its crested throat is signified its twofold devotion in prayer, namely for its own salvation and for that of others. In its golden neck, holy exhortation; in its purple rear part, the imitation of Christ's passion is expressed.

The falcon turns its neck in a full circle with a single motion, its breast remaining unmoved, so much so that its two eyes seem, by a kind of natural discernment, equal to the hundred eyes of Argus. It watches carefully for prey even behind its own back. It has weak kidneys, a strong breast, and, less than other birds, wants to be fed with delicacies while being carried. It flies with great violence and is less cautious in guarding itself. In hunting the heron, when two falcons are released, they fly together as partners: one climbs to the greatest height, the other flies low near the ground, so that the one climbing high may knock the flying heron down by striking it, and the one flying low may catch it as it falls. There are two kinds of falcon: one ignoble, which catches a bird only through much toil and training conditioning it to it; the other noble, which catches a bird naturally with little practice. The first kind, considered the baser, when it has driven a heron to the ground and is on the point of catching it, sees the heron disgorge from its mouth an eel or some fish it had swallowed, and at once the ignoble falcon lets the captured heron fly free into the open air, and instead swiftly seizes the offered, foul gift. The noble falcon does not act this way; rather it scorns the gift cast up by the heron and presses on more fiercely to catch and punish the deceiver. The ignoble falcon signifies wicked prelates of the Church, or deans, or even secular judges, who, once they have taken money, release the guilty, letting sins go unpunished, 'justifying the wicked for a bribe' in a detestable manner, according to Isaiah. The falcon has a sharp, hard bone in its breast, which nature gave it, providently, for striking its prey. A falcon is best in its second or third molt. The wild hawk may be allowed to fast a great deal, and it grows very tame this way.
The coot, as Ambrose reports, feeds the eagle's young cast down from the nest, with a reverent mercy, together with its own young — setting an example concerning hospitality to strangers.

Griffins are birds, as Jacques says, savage beyond measure, with bodies so large that they overcome and kill armed men in battle. For they have very large, hooked claws, with which they tear apart men and beasts. They are of such capacity that cups fit for human use are made from them. This creature is four-footed, with a head and wings like an eagle's, but much larger, and in the rest of its body resembles a lion, and dwells in the Hyperborean mountains, being especially hostile to horses and to men.
As the Experimentator says, it places an agate stone in its nest, and there is no doubt this is for some remedial purpose. It is clear, then, that stones are given by God for some remedial purpose.
Griffins, as Hrabanus says, are said to dig up gold and to delight in the sight of what they have dug up.

A greedy bird brings forth its young early in spring, when other birds are wont to anticipate their conceiving. Whence it happens that 'an inheritance hastily gotten...' and so on, for the eggs are spoiled through the winter.

The 'gracocenderon' is a bird of the East, said to be endowed with wondrous chastity and restraint. For this bird, among all the living creatures of the earth, accomplishes its own generation with the least mating; for it mates only once a year, and this for the sake of offspring, and so it is free of all lust. Let man, then, endowed with reason, blush for shame, who mates indiscriminately at every season and has no measure of that restraint, but instead exhausts his feeble body with lust and shortens his life through excessive indulgence.

Cranes are birds that fly in an ordered, letter-like formation. Pliny, Solinus, Jacques, Ambrose, and Isidore describe the crane. Whenever they set out on their expeditions, they go out under a kind of military standard. For the one that leads the whole flight corrects the others with her voice, so that they do not break formation. When she grows hoarse, another takes over, appointed to the same duty. By night they divide watches among themselves, so that every tenth one stays sleepless. Those keeping watch hold small stones while standing on one leg lifted from the ground; when it slips, since they want to sleep, they wake and cry out. They sleep with the head tucked under a wing, resting alternately on each leg; the leader, neck erect, keeps watch and looks about.

Cranes, as the Experimentator says, if they see clouds gathering, cry out and urge the leader to catch a swifter flight. When they land on the ground to eat, their leader raises her head, to keep watch over them all, while the rest eat without a care. If she sees a man, she cries out to warn the unwary ones. Cranes flying set themselves against the wind. They have a single internal passage. About to cross the sea, they swallow sand. They sometimes have a stone in the stomach which they vomit up. Of this stone, those who have tried it say that this stone, with the help of fire, turns into gold.

Solinus: they swallow sand so as to keep an even weight; they also pick up small stones with their feet for the same reason. But when they know they have reached the middle of their crossing, they free their feet of the burden of stones. Sailors have reported this, having often been showered from that very fall with a rain of stones. They do not vomit up the sand until they have found a safe place to settle. If one grows tired, all of them gather round and lift her up, until she recovers her strength through rest. They turn black with age. Tame cranes are used to catch others. And whichever one is now in front during flight will, without ill will, be behind in turn.
According to Aristotle, fearing winter, they flee beyond Egypt and there fight against men a cubit tall who are called Pygmies, and this is no fable, as Aristotle says.

Or, as the Gloss on that passage of Ezekiel says: 'the Pygmy people were in your towers,' meaning that such a people exists in the regions of the East. Such men are also short-lived. The battle of cranes is so stubborn and fierce that they can be caught by hand. The female crane stands still when mounted by the male in mating.

When the cock is about to crow, he shakes his wings, so as to rouse himself more fully. In the depths of night he crows more strongly; in the morning, more gently. By his crowing he calms horses, spurs camels on, and is even said to drive away phantoms. Many herbs that nourish the cock kill other animals. About to sleep he climbs high and rests on one leg. The lion fears a white cock. According to Aristotle, he crows after a fight and after victory — the male, not the female, gives voice. Like the cock and the quail, on seeing its own image in a mirror, it wastes away its strength [attacking it]. With a soft murmur he calls his hens to eat pure grain. It sometimes happens that, once he has grown old, he lays an egg, which a toad broods, and from this a certain kind of basilisk is produced. When his hens die, the cock, wasting away with grief, abstains from crowing out of sorrow. A castrated cock is called a capon; it is called 'pepo' in scripture, but commonly 'capo.' It does not crow nor breed — like a bad cleric.
Isaiah: 'Shebna, the steward of the household, is like a capon.'

Jacques and the Lapidarius say that, once castrated after three years of life and then left to live another five or six years, a cock carries in its liver a precious stone called 'alectorius,' and once it has conceived this stone in its liver, it never drinks again. Hence, if someone holds this stone in his mouth, it quenches thirst.

The hen, as Augustine says, is a bird most attentive to her chicks. She gathers them under her wings and warms them, and generally defends and protects them against kites, though sometimes proud chicks that shun her soft wings become prey to birds of prey.
Jacques: her eggs are taken from the hen every day, and yet she does not therefore stop laying, provided you leave her one. But hens that exceed the proper measure of laying die quickly.
John: when they lay eggs in a hidden place, however, they rise up crying out and so betray them to plunderers.

A hen carries, on the right side of her belly, the eggs that will hatch males, and on the left side, those that will hatch females. Eggs round at the pointed end produce females; long eggs, sharply pointed at the end, produce males; the elongated ones have a finer flavor. All birds, unlike other animals, are born feet-first.

As the Experimentator says, a hen labors greatly in laying, and yet, according to the philosopher John, sings after laying, according to the saying: 'a woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow.' Brooding is best before the spring equinox; after the solstice it does not reach its full measure, and the later it is, the smaller the result.

Pliny: on the day a hen lays an egg, she does not die from an asp's bite — indeed it is a medicine for those who have been struck. So then, do some good thing every day, however small, so that by this means you may be protected from the harm of the threatening enemy. There is a test in water for which eggs should be set to hatch chicks: an empty egg placed in water floats, but a full one sinks and is the one that should be set. Incubation should begin after the new moon, since eggs begun earlier more often fail. If it suddenly thunders, they often fail, and hearing a hawk's cry spoils them too. A remedy against thunder is an iron nail placed crosswise through the eggs, or straight through inside them. Pliny: if you melt gold and also mix in parts of a hen, they consume the gold within themselves, so that it could be said that hens are the poison of gold. The yolk of an egg laid at the full moon removes every stain from a woolen garment, if you rub it in well and then wash it.

Aristotle: most hook-taloned birds lay few eggs. The same: long, sharp-pointed eggs produce males; round eggs, and those round even at the pointed end, produce females. The young form, however, at the pointed end. The same: eggs have two colors; the beginning of generation is from the white, nourishment from the yolk. The same: eggs can only be fertile if conceived by mating with a male and penetrated by his spirit. The same: the chick is fully formed in ten days after the egg's generation; the broad end emerges first, then the pointed end. Every kind of bird is born twice. First the eggs are laid, and then they are shaped and given life by the heat of the mother's body. The same: thunder spoils eggs during incubation. Eggs are said to have such power that if wood is soaked in it, it will not burn; mixed together, it is also said to glue broken pieces of glass. The same: egg white dropped into a thick liquid, like syrup, thins and refines it.

Chicks of hens are produced from eggs warmed in an oven, without any brooding by the mother; hence, however many eggs one has, one can have that many chicks in a single day by this method, if one wishes.

Aristotle: a certain drinker placed eggs under his pillow and said he would keep on drinking until chicks were hatched from them. The same: a hen lays at every season except during the two months of the solstices. The same: hens that lay excessively die quickly. Generally: if hens do not brood their own eggs, they fall ill. Fed half-cooked barley, they are often induced to lay larger eggs.
A hen's eggs should be set to hatch as the moon is waxing.

The 'gallus gallinacius,' as the Book of Nature says, is a castrated cock, which scripture calls 'pepo' but we call 'capo'; it is said that, since they are not restrained by lust, they fatten more quickly.

This bird, as the Experimentator says, fattens up living with hens, but never impregnates or fertilizes them; it feeds with them, but does not defend them. It does not crow, nor does it mark the hours of day or night. Such birds are good for nothing but the kitchen. Their flesh is more nourishing than that of any other fowl, for it produces good blood and is excellent nourishment.

On this, the master of the Order of Preachers, Jordan of blessed memory, said in a certain sermon, speaking to canons and clerics at a synod: 'Shebna the scribe,' he said, 'will be carried off like a capon. And to where? To no place but the devil's kitchen. And why? Because it does not breed, nor crow, nor defend. It breeds no spiritual children — and would that it bred no carnal ones either! It does not sing the canonical hours — and would that it sang no jester's songs or trifles either! It defends its little sheep neither by prayer, nor by preaching, nor by ecclesiastical censure. It is, then, a hireling, who, seeing the wolf coming, flees, and is therefore good for nothing but the devil's kitchen.' Together with him will be carried off all who call themselves canons, or provosts, or clerics, without producing the fruit they owe.

Jacques and the Lapidarius: they are sometimes castrated once they have lived three years, and then allowed to live five or six years more, and so a precious stone called 'electorius' is found in their liver. So then, once they have conceived this stone in the liver, they never drink again afterward. Hence, if someone holds this stone in his mouth, it quenches thirst.

The wood-cock, also called the pheasant by Pliny — and the name 'gallicus' fits it well too — is a most beautiful bird. It lacks a crest on its head and spurs on its legs; yet, deprived of these weapons, it is nonetheless known to be a bold bird. Knowing this, fowlers make a shield of white linen cloth, in the middle of which they place a small patch of red cloth. Gazing intently at this redness against the white, the cock fixes his eye and marvels at this strange sight; and without delay, the fowler, seeing him transfixed by the sight, forces him to retreat backward by pressing forward with the shield, until he drives the captive bird into nets set up ready at a distance. And this is how the wood-cock is caught. It signifies those who, led by curiosity of sight, fall little by little into the devil's nets, following the example of Dinah and David.

Alexander says the pheasant is caught this way: a fowler, covered with a cloth on which this bird is painted, shows himself to the pheasant, who, following or pursuing the covered man, now retreating, now fleeing, at last is caught in a net by the fowler's companion, who lies hidden in ambush.

As the Experimentator says, this bird hides its head by driving its beak into the ground, and so believes itself entirely hidden. In rainy weather it grows sad and then hides in brambles and woods; around evening or dawn it comes out of the woods and is then easily hunted. It sheds its feathers from fatness and renews itself again. Its flesh is finer and more delicate than that of other woodland birds.

The jay, as Isidore says, is named from its chattering ['garrulitas']. For it is the most talkative kind of bird, and tiresome in its cries. It passes from chattering at one thing to another, and there is scarcely anyone it will not chatter at as he passes. It is said to imitate the voices and melodies of other birds not for the pleasure of joy but for the sake of chatter, as though mocking them. This bird, caught young, is caged, so that it may be taught to speak articulate words; and once it has escaped, it chatters all the more. But it sometimes happens that, while it pays no heed to itself and is intent on its chattering, a sparrowhawk snatches it unawares. This bird is marked by such a variety of plumage that it is said to lack no color found in other birds.
It is often said to go mad, so much so that the Experimentator says that, out of excessive fury, it hangs itself, raging, in the forked branches of a tree.

The jackdaw is a bird of the crow family, though smaller in body. It gladly nests in the high branches of trees, and in such numbers that as many as seven pairs of jackdaws often build their nests in a single tree; for these birds get along together with one another very well. It is an extremely noisy bird, especially at mating time. And when spring weather stirs mating, the male, for love's sake, feeds the female. The flesh of its young is edible, especially once skinned.

The ibis is a bird that feeds on serpents and their eggs; hence, meeting in the air the winged snakes that come from Arabia, before they descend into neighboring provinces, it devours them. The venom of these serpents is so swift that death follows the bite before the pain does. This bird conceives and gives birth through the mouth, as Solinus says.

Whoever eats its eggs dies. Isidore: it cleanses itself with its beak, pouring water onto its rear parts. It walks by night and day along the shores of the sea and of other waters; it never, however, enters the water itself, but delights only in the carcasses cast up there, both of fish and of other animals.

Note the verse [on declension patterns, using] horses, dogs, oxen, sheep, goats, pigs, she-goats: 'the ibis is a bird, the asp-serpent is the ibix, and the ibis is envious, from eo, is, it.' This one makes 'ibidis' [in the genitive], that makes 'ibicis,' this makes 'ibis.' The ibex, genitive 'ibicis,' is a wild goat, whose home is among the rocks. The ibex is an animal; the ibis a bird, and the ibis is envious.

The swallow feeds in flight on gnats, flies, and small bees. Isidore: it is never molested by birds of ill omen, as though sacred. When their young's eyes are troubled, the mothers apply celandine as a medicine.
Pliny: this bird, which has no talons, lives on flesh. They fly across the seas and spend the winter there.
As the Experimentator says, they have little flesh, and it is dark; many feathers and large wings, and so they have swift flight. Its blood, drawn from beneath the right wing, heals the eyes.
Solinus: it has foreknowledge, such that it leaves a roof that is about to collapse and does not seek out high places [that are unsafe].

Many swallows carry gems in their breast, as the Book of Nature says. This gem is sometimes found black, sometimes reddish, and is called 'celidonius.' It benefits the moon-struck and drives away harmful humors; washed in water, it heals sick eyes. Those swallow chicks that have this stone are recognized in this way, if, as a sign of peace, they sit in the nest facing beak to beak; the remaining chicks, which do not have it, sit with their backs turned to each other. Swallow dung has a most effective power to blind, if it falls into the eyes — an example from Tobit.

Pliny: swallow chicks are blind at first; the females conceive by the mere fancy of lust. If someone blinds swallow chicks, their eyes grow back again, as Aristotle, Pliny, and Adelinus say. Swallows, as Pliny says, are untrainable, as are mice, whereas lions and elephants can be tamed and domesticated. It lays twice a year, as Aristotle says, but its eggs are ruined in winter by the cold.

We call the 'isida' bird this from the sound of its cry. It has only two toes, with hooked claws on its foot, but a small, straight beak. It is indeed a small bird, but most brilliant in the beauty of its feathers. It is commonly believed of this bird that, if you strip the feathered skin from this bird once dead and fix the stripped skin to a wall, the skin will change its feathers every year, just as if it were still on a living body. This signifies those who, while living, were unwilling to abandon their old habits and evil customs, which they will indeed exchange only in death, since instead of delights they will obtain punishment, instead of joy, sorrow, and instead of passing goods, eternal punishment.

The 'kiche' bird cries out with varied voices, and changes its cry almost every day. The young of this bird, once strong enough to fly, feed their parents in old age, and let them live in the nests without any labor of their own.

The gull is a bird, as the Gloss says, endowed with a double nature. This bird, as the Gloss says, dwells both in water and on land, and delights in both elements: swimming in the water, flying in the air.

The nightingale is a bird, as Ambrose reports in the Hexaemeron. While she broods her eggs, she eases the long labor of the night with the sweetness of her song, and this, as it seems to Ambrose, is the bird's intent: that she may, no less by the sweetness of her notes than by the warmth of her body, bring life to the eggs she broods.
Blessed Augustine and many others have reported something similar of the lion.

The kite is so named from its lightness ['mollis'] in strength and flight, yet it is most rapacious and always lies in wait for domestic animals. It resembles the hawk in claws, feet, and beak, but has curved wings rather than the straight ones of the hawk. As the Experimentator says: the kite is bold with small creatures, timid with large ones. It is put to flight by the sparrowhawk, though it is three times its size. The kite cannot molt its feathers unless it drinks the salt waters of the sea, facing southward.
Hence, when the time of its change comes, leaving the land where it dwells, it seeks that region: 'the kite in the sky knows her appointed time.'

'Meauce' are sea birds larger than ducks, as the Book of Nature says, named from the sound of their cry. For the 'meauca' cries constantly, and is most greedy for carrion, especially human carrion. As a storm approaches, it cries out most, as though rejoicing then at the prospect of prey from the dead. It attacks the eye first in a corpse. It lies in wait for small animals, wherever they are gathered.

The blackbird, as Jacques says, was in ancient times called 'modula,' because it modulates its song. It produces marvelous varieties of song, especially when it senses spring approaching; for in wintertime it is silent, mute. A domesticated blackbird, against its own nature, eats meat, and it sings the more sweetly for this. In winter, from its fatness, it can scarcely fly. It gladly bathes and cleans its feathers with its beak, though it is a plain and black bird. The blackbird turns from black to reddish. It changes its beak to whiteness each year. There is also another kind, but much larger. These, called 'goat-milkers' from what they do, enter the stables of goatherds and fly at the udders for the sake of the milk's substance; by this harm the goat's udder dies and the goats go blind. These birds are sometimes said to lack sight themselves.

The jackdaw, as Jacques says, is named as though 'taking coin' or 'loving coin.' For if it finds gold or silver, it steals it and hides it. Its flesh provokes an itching of the head; hence it too desires to have its own head scratched.

The diving-bird gets its name from its constant diving. Often submerged in the depths, as Ambrose says, they gather signs of coming winds beneath the waves, and, foreseeing a storm at sea, flee to the shore with cries. When a diving-bird is about to be struck, it dives underwater, and it signifies those who make excuses when reproved in confession.
As the Experimentator says, in winter they are fatter, because of their lack of movement. For every animal delights in clear weather and roams more freely in it than in stormy weather.

The sparrowhawk is a noble bird, as the Book of Nature says, smaller in form and strength than the gyrfalcon, though both have the same color of plumage. Yet they refuse to fly together as companions; for it is said to be envious and proud.

The sparrowhawk disdains and pursues its own kind as it would a bird of another species, and this contrary to the way of all other birds, since, as Aristotle says, every bird that catches prey in flight spares birds of its own kind. The sparrowhawk alone, then, lacks this decency — sharing this trait with man himself, who among quadrupeds does not cease to prey upon animals of his own kind. In winter the sparrowhawk holds a captured bird alive under its feet all night against the cold, mindful, as the common people say, of the favor it has received; in the morning it lets the captive fly free. A memorable and pious example! Woe to those who not only fail to return good for good, but even repay good with evil!
The 'nicticorax,' as Adelinus says, means 'raven of the night,' indeed a bird we call the night-owl. It loves the darkness of night.

[This bird], startled, flies and cries out, lives on human filth, and sings against evil, and hates the light. This bird begins to grow more watchful and seek food precisely when other animals give themselves to sleep; if it flew by day, it would be attacked by other birds. It has a huge head, not shaped like other birds'; it has a hooked beak like the sparrowhawk's, and hooked, rough claws on its feet. There is a cunning contest of the owls against other birds.

Pliny: when attacked by man or by birds, it lies on its back and defends itself with its beak and the talons of its feet. The hawk, however, comes to its aid by a certain natural alliance and shares the fight with it. If a night-owl is ever brought to the island of Crete, it dies at once. Its flesh helps paralytics.

The pelican ['onocrotalus'] is a long-beaked bird dwelling in the regions of the East. When it wishes to make a sound, it places its head in the water, and so gives forth a voice like a braying roar. There are two kinds of them, one aquatic, the other of the wilderness. This bird alone among others lacks a spleen, as Aristotle says.

Isidore, however, says that this bird stores up much food at once in its belly, and in this it signifies the greedy, of whom Job says: 'the riches he devoured...' and so on. Afterward, when hungry, it draws the food out and eats it again.

As the Experimentator says, it has a kind of pouch in its throat, in which it first places the food, and after an hour sends what it has received into a second stomach. For it has two stomachs, one of which is in the gullet; in the other it cooks and digests the food. This is not so in other birds.

The pelican gets its name as though having 'grey skin' ['pellem canam']. Hence Augustine and Isidore say it has grey feathers. This bird dwells in Egypt; it is often found near the Nile. This bird loves its young and delights in them, but they in turn try to peck out its eyes. For this reason it kills its young, but then strips itself of its feathery garment, afflicted with no small grief for three days. It opens its side with its beak and, with its own blood, brings its bloodied young back to life. It is said that it does this precisely when it finds its young killed by a serpent that had lain in wait for them. There are two kinds of pelicans, one aquatic, which lives on fish, the other dwells on land and feeds on serpents. The pelican lives on the milk of the crocodile, which that beast, because of the excessive fullness of its teats, discharges in some marshy place; hence the pelican also gladly follows the crocodile. Or, as others say, it is called 'pellicanus' because its skin, when handled, seems to become grey ['canere']. This bird is lean, because, it is said, with its intestine stretched taut through its inward parts, it passes through whatever food it takes in without any digestion. From this it happens that it is satisfied with the least amount of its own fat, being nourished by the smallest amount of juice.

The 'porphyrio,' as the philosopher John says, is a bird outside the habit and manner of other birds; for it has one broad foot for swimming, and another cloven for walking, and in this note that it enjoys both elements, swimming in water like ducks and walking on land like partridges.
The 'porphyrio' alone, as Pliny says, apart from the parrot, takes up water in its foot as though in a hand and carries it to its beak, and drinks and feeds itself in the manner of man.

The peacock is a most beautiful bird, a friend of beauty and cleanliness, as Aristotle says. It has a long, eyed tail, a sapphire-colored breast, and likewise a sapphire-colored neck. By its cry it drives away all venomous animals, which do not dare remain wherever they hear the peacock's voice. Its voice is terrible, its gait simple and as though furtive.
Augustine says that the flesh of a dead peacock does not rot or stink for a whole year, in the book On the City of God. The same teacher also says it never rots at all.
Jacques: when the peacock is looked at and praised, it spreads its tail out in a circle, arching it, and displays its beauty, especially facing the sun, since the colors then shine more brilliantly.
The Book of Nature: the peacock, with tail spread, on seeing the ugliness of its own feet, lowers its outspread tail.
Pliny: it begins to pour out its jewel-like colors from the age of three years, and then breeds.

The peacock, having lost its tail each year, ashamed and grieving, seeks hiding places along with the falling leaves of trees, until it grows back. When the peacock has kept watch at night and cannot see itself set in darkness, it cries out in fear, believing it has lost its beauty. The males break the eggs out of desire for their mates, who would otherwise be occupied in brooding; for this reason the females lay in hiding. When the peacock climbs high, it is a sign of rain. The peacock, on Aristotle's testimony, is envious; it does not deign to recognize its own offspring until it recognizes itself, resembled, in the crest of the young.

The partridge gets its name from its cry; hence Jacques, Ambrose, and Isidore say that this bird is so deceitful and cunning that it steals and broods another's eggs. But the deceit does not succeed. For when the chicks hear the voice of their true mother, by a certain natural instinct they abandon the one who brooded them and return to the one who bore them. The partridge, however, has a drier brain than other birds, and as a consequence it is forgetful, and so, forgetting its own nest, it loses its eggs, which are then seized and brooded by another. When someone approaches their nests, the mothers come forward of their own accord to those approaching and, feigning weakness of foot or wing, as though they might be caught at any moment, pretend to walk more slowly. By this lie they distract those they meet, until they are drawn far enough from the nests. When the chicks fear being caught, they lift up clods of earth with their feet and hide themselves beneath them.

When males fight over females, the defeated ones are mounted by the victors in an unnatural mating, and, as the Experimentator says, headlong lust forgets which sex is which. When they are caught in a fowler's woven snare, one follows another without recognizing the misery, nor does the one following draw back from the danger of the one already caught, deceived by the company of its fellows — apply this as an example of a perverse pattern. At night they sit with their backs turned to each other; female partridges are so stirred by lust that they are said to conceive by scent alone. For if the wind blows from the male, the females are impregnated. At mating time, tongues extended toward one another, they burn with the desire for mating. What we have said of partridges, namely that they conceive from the wind, we also assert of doves, geese, peacocks, and hens. The breast, together with the upper parts, is very tasty, but the lower parts are not so.
Pliny: partridge gall mixed in equal measure with honey is good for clearing the eyes.

[The plovers] are birds the size of the partridge; they are adorned with varied feathers, marked with saffron, white, and black. They are said to live on air alone, and yet are fat. The proof that they live on air is this, that although they grow fat, nothing can ever be found in their entrails.

The magpie is a most cunning bird, as Pliny says. The flesh of its young is given to sharpen the eyesight of those who eat it, though unless it has first been skinned, it does not easily yield to cooking. It makes up for the shortness of its wings with a longer tail. It builds its nest with two openings; through one it enters, through the other it puts out its tail. Pliny: it is certain that in the month of August they are driven to a kind of madness and sometimes hang themselves in the brambles among the thorn bushes. It watches over the courtyards or gardens where it nests and betrays the ambushes of those lurking there with much crying out. Caught young, it learns to speak words; it sometimes dies, overcome by the difficulty of a word.

The sparrow, sitting on the ground, before taking flight, strikes the ground with its foot and then lifts itself into the air. It is quickly roused to fury, but there is no lasting quarrel, as the Experimentator says. Sparrows are hotter than all other birds. Hence they are astringent and stimulate the blood, and are lustful beyond measure, whence it also gets its name from 'suffering' [i.e., a Latin pun on 'passer']. Its dung is very hot when discharged, but cools very quickly, and signifies those who believe 'for a time,' and so on. It digests quickly whatever it swallows, and so the food it takes does not fatten it at all, but only sustains it.

In certain regions sparrows suffer the falling sickness, and this, as Aristotle believes, because they eat henbane seed. They steal the dove's nest. When the young of sparrows must first fly out, neighboring sparrows, together with their own parents, accompany the flight of the weak fledglings, supporting them by their close gathering.

The nightingale is said to delight so much in the pleasantness of her own voice that she very rarely eats, and when she does, does so with the greatest haste. She sings only in springtime, never in winter. She is said to delight in her songs so stubbornly and heedlessly that she would rather waste away and lose her life than be deprived of the modulation of her voice. Hence she is called 'philomena,' from 'philos,' which means love, and 'menos,' which means failing, as though 'failing from love.' Note that, as soon as the nightingale begins to mate, she at once loses the pleasantness of her voice and, as Pliny says, her voice becomes different, and her color changes too. She sometimes indulges in lust with the sparrow and lets herself be mounted by him. The thinness of their tongues is not found in other birds.

The parrot is a bird of India, as Jacques and Solinus say, green in color, with a reddish, that is golden, collar, and a large, broad tongue; hence it utters articulate words, so that, if you do not see it, you might think a man was speaking. It greets a man, saying 'Ave' or 'Chaire.' In its first and second year it learns more quickly and retains more firmly. Its beak is so hard that, when it falls from a height onto a rock, it catches itself with the force of its mouth, using its beak as a kind of foundation. Its head, however, is so tough that, when men force it to imitate human speech, it must be struck with a small iron rod while being taught. It feeds itself with its foot and brings food to its mouth as a man does with his hand. They are said to nest on Mount Gilboa, precisely because it never or rarely rains there; for they cannot bear rain. They tolerate other waters in some measure, but die from rain. It guards its tail with the greatest care and cleans its feathers with its beak quite often. The nobler ones have five toes on their feet, the baser only three.
As Aristotle says, they drink wine, and it is an exceedingly lustful bird; small wonder, since it gladly drinks wine, in which lust resides.
Philosophus: when made drunk with wine, it takes great delight in gazing at a virgin.

The ostrich is a bird, as Isidore says, called 'assida' in Greek; it is also called 'camelon,' because it has feet like a camel's. This bird, when the time comes for it to lay its eggs, raises its eyes to the sky to see whether the star called Vergiliae has risen; for it does not lay its eggs on the ground unless that star has risen, and the reason is this: in the season of summer, when the crops flower, around July, the star Vergiliae rises in the sky, and then indeed the ostrich digs in the ground and lays its eggs there and covers them with sand. Once they are covered, it leaves the place and at once forgets the eggs it has just laid, and never returns to them again. For it is by nature forgetful, and so it breeds in the hot season and covers the eggs in the sandy ground, so that what it would otherwise have had to do by sitting and brooding, the calm of the season and the mildness of the air instead provide for it. So then, the eggs warmed by the sand, which is heated by the sun, produce the chicks. This bird has feathers like the hawk's and the gyrfalcon's, but is slow in flight. It eats and digests iron, since it is of the hottest nature. It hates and pursues the horse by nature; the horse, in turn, fears and hates it so much that it does not dare even to look at it. These birds run so fast on the ground that they outstrip horses in speed. In running they raise their wings; their feathers are like hair, and their wings are slight; they have eyelids. They have cloven claws for grasping stones, which they hurl at their pursuers while fleeing. Their foolishness is so great that, when they hide their heads in a bush, they believe the rest of their body's bulk is hidden too. It is also said to look at the sky with one eye and at the earth with the other. It has a large, broad breastbone shaped like a shield, and this was made for it to protect its large body; for it has a body nearly as large as a donkey of medium build.
It naturally goes bald, as Pliny says, but has a very tough skin, by which, unfeathered, it is protected from the harshness of the cold.

The screech-owl, as Isidore says, gets its name from its cry; for when it screeches, it shrieks. Hence Lucan says: 'what the warm owl and the nocturnal screech-owl are said to complain of.' The screech-owl, then, is a night bird, and is popularly called 'anima,' from loving, for it loves its little ones. This bird alone, contrary to the custom of other birds, is said to drip a kind of milky fluid into its young.

Starlings are small birds, as Pliny says, built for flying. They gleam with a dusky color. They fly in flocks and wheel about in a kind of ball-shaped circle, all straining toward the center, and this because of hawks, which lie in wait for them. They gather at evening and murmur together in immense crowds.
Silent through the night, they raise a murmur when dawn reddens the sky; then, divided, they fly off in bands to feed.

The 'trogopale,' as Solinus says, is a bird found in Ethiopia. It is larger than the eagle, having horns like a ram; hence it carries an armed head against all birds hostile to it, fiercely driving them off. It is of a rust-colored hue. It has a head like the phoenix's, except that it carries an armed head, as we have said.

The turtledove, according to Aristotle, is of remarkable chastity; it loves its mate and keeps faith with it alone, so much so that, once it dies, it does not join with another, but goes about alone, perching on the dry branches of trees, mourning and sorrowful. In place of song it has moaning. It is hostile to no bird, but is most patient against the harassment of all birds. It builds its nest from very few branches, in which it rests and broods its eggs.

The turtledove, as Ambrose says, throws squill leaves over its nest, so that no hostile animal attacks its young; for it knows that venomous animals flee the leaves of this plant. The blood of its right wing is medicinal when applied to the eyes. In a south wind they cannot fly well.

The bat is named as though 'using its wing at evening,' as the Book of Nature says; for it flies only in the evening and at night. In winter it hides; it has no plumage on its body, no feathers on its wings, and differs in shape from a mouse in nothing, since it alone among birds gives birth and suckles its young at the teat in the manner of livestock, except that it has a tail and wings shaped like a bird's, though these bear no feathers at all, but only membranes spread out like a kind of leathery, pliant skin.

Its blood, with thistle, is a chief remedy against snakebite, as Pliny says. He also says that it seeks out noise, and that its blood removes hair. It has teeth, which we do not usually find in other birds. In India there are bats larger than doves, having, as it were, human teeth, with which they strike men in the face, cutting off their nose, ears, and other members.

The screech-owl ['ulula'] is a bird, as Isidore says, named from wailing and mourning; for when it cries, it imitates either weeping or moaning. Hence it is falsely held among augurs that, if it wails, it foretells sorrow, and if silent, prosperity.

The hoopoe is a bird forbidden by the Law; as Isidore says, it is an unclean bird that builds its nest in dung, and dwells more gladly in foul places. Yet it is quite a beautiful bird, and is crested with certain feathers standing up like a helmet. In winter it hides and is silent; in spring it appears again, with only one persistent call, like the cuckoo. As their parents age, they shed their feathers in the nest among their now-grown young, and are fed by their young, until they recover their strength and their feathers.

The Physiologus says there is another mark of devotion in them toward their parents. For when the parents lose their sight from old age, the young by nature gather a certain known herb and anoint their parents' blinded eyes with it, so that by the herb's remedy they recover the health of their eyes.

Jacques: if someone, going to sleep, anoints his temples with the blood of a hoopoe, he will see, as it were, demons strangling him in his dreams. A hoopoe's heart is useful to sorcerers and enchanters.

The vulture is a bird whose feathers, if placed in fire, produce a smoke whose smell drives away serpents, as Pliny says. The same: those who keep a vulture's heart at their side are safe from the attack of wild beasts, serpents, and crawling things. Vultures, like eagles, sense carcasses across the sea.

Isidore: it goes first for the eye in a carcass. It follows armies, so as to gorge on the corpses of the dead; it delights in quarrels, hatred, and wars. When a vulture has grown up and sees its mother old and too weak to fly, it kills and destroys her. But if some other bird, even a stronger one, tries to seize its young, it exposes itself to danger, striking with its wings and wounding with its claws. The mother forbids her cast-out young, once they are able to fly, to come near the places where they were born, jealous, that is, over food, since a single pair of vultures occupies a large territory. It does not hunt in the areas near its nest, but far away, so as not to stir up the hatred of neighboring peoples against itself. When it hunts something, it does not carry off the prey at once, but first tests its weight, and only then, having judged it, carries it.
Hrabanus: some say that vultures do not come together in mating, but conceive and breed without coupling, and that their offspring live nearly up to a hundred years.

Pliny: the vulture hunts from midday until night, and rests from sunrise until midday. When it grows old, its beak lengthens above, so much that its curve reaches the lower lip, and so it happens that, unable to open its beak, it dies of hunger and starvation; for it does not dash its beak against a rock, as the eagle does, nor does it know how to relieve the trouble, and so it dies. Some say a dying vulture swallows its own brain out of spite, that is, so that it will not be of use to men, since it is said to be effective against paralysis. If it sees its young growing fat too quickly, it wounds their feet with its beak, so as to keep them lean. It fights with the gyrfalcon and rushes at it, but, since the gyrfalcon is agile, it yields to the vulture's violent charge, and the vulture, being heavy with the impetus and unable to check itself, kills itself. Since the vulture indiscriminately descends on every carcass, it does not avoid dangers and traps.

Vultures, by certain signs, as Ambrose says, seem to announce the deaths of men. For when opposing armies of men prepare for war between themselves, vultures follow them in great flocks, showing that a great multitude of men is about to fall in the war and become their prey.

The 'abides' is a sea animal, as Aristotle says, which is at first aquatic, and its nourishment is in salt water. Then this animal's form changes and becomes another, and then, leaving the water, it is nourished on land. Then its name too changes, and it is called 'astoas,' and it is remarkable in this, that just as its bodily form changes, so too the very nature of its habits changes.

The 'achune' is a monster of the sea, as Aristotle says. This animal is greedier than all other sea creatures; it lives on prey, and whatever it eats turns into the thickness of its own body. Hence its belly extends beyond all reckoning and proper proportion to the size of its body. When afflicted by hunger, it devours its own flesh, choosing to be partly consumed itself rather than become entirely consumed as prey to other beasts. This animal lacks a stomach, and so, when it has eaten, its belly swells greatly, and when its belly can stretch no further, it vomits fish out through its mouth, and this easily, since its mouth adjoins its belly directly, having no neck, as is the case with other sea animals; for no fish has a neck. The 'achune,' as Aristotle says, curls itself up like a hedgehog out of fear of hunters, and when it senses that the danger will not let up, driven by hunger it devours its own flesh, choosing to be partly consumed rather than be entirely consumed by another beast.
The 'barchora,' as Aristotle says, is a sea animal that eats small fish. The mouth of this animal is stronger than the mouth of any other animal, for if it takes a stone in its mouth, it breaks it.

The crocodile is a four-footed animal that thrives equally on land and in the sea, as Jacques, Solinus, and Pliny say. By day it rests most often on land, and this so motionlessly that, unless you knew its habit beforehand, you would think it dead, luring birds with its open jaws for the sake of food; by night, however, it stays in the water. It lacks a tongue; the gape of its mouth reaches back to its ears, and it moves its upper jaw. It feigns sleep with its eyes closed, keeping its mouth wide open. And it kills and swallows the birds that descend as though for food. In this it signifies usurers, who invite poor merchants to borrow and then devour them. The crocodile is armed with the enormity of its claws. In winter it takes no food. When it has killed a man, it mourns him. When its heart is torn out, the crocodile lives on for a while afterward, which indeed goes against every animal that has its life from its heart.

The 'cricos' is a sea animal, as Aristotle says. It has two cleavings at the end of its foot, which make three toes on three hoof-like claws. It has a small right foot and a large left one, and for this reason, when it walks, it carries its whole body on the left foot. In stormy weather it grows weak, and in the stirring of the winds it clings to rocks and does not move. Such are those who fear persecution.

The 'chylon' is a sea animal, as Aristotle says. This animal, among all kinds of animals, does not graze, but is nourished only by its own moisture, which flows from it. This moisture is viscous, and the animal takes it alone as its nourishment; hence this animal is always fasting and yet strong in body. We observe that women can bear fasting longer, going many days without eating, more than men can, and this because of the moist and viscous excess humors, of which women have a greater abundance than men.

Sea-dogs are marine beasts, as Pliny says, terrible for their breath and their hostility. For they are enemies to every living thing that falls beneath their attack. They hunt through the sea great numbers and shoals of fish, like dogs hunting wild game on land, except that they cannot bark, but instead of barking have a horrible breath.

The sea-dragon is a cruel monster. Like a land dragon it is stretched out in length, but it lacks wings. It has a twisting tail, and a head small in proportion to its body. Its bite is deadly to fish, to other sea creatures, and to man. It has fins in place of wings, which it uses in swimming. It crosses great stretches of sea in a single burst, and this by the strength of its own power rather than by the oarage of its fins. The ash of its bones cures toothache.

Dolphins do not have their mouths in the place other sea creatures do, but in their bellies. Contrary to the nature of aquatic creatures, they alone move their tongues. They have spiny tongues along the back, which bristle up when the creatures are angered; but when they are calm, these are covered by certain sheaths. They have no visible trace of a sense of smell, though they smell very keenly. They live one hundred and forty years, and this, the Experimentator says, once their tails have been cut off.
Dolphins delight in music; they excel in remarkable speed. The dolphin alone, as Aristotle says, lacks a gall bladder.

If someone eats dolphin flesh, as the Experimentator says, and falls into the sea, if he is found by dolphins, they will at once devour him; but if he has not eaten it, they lift him up on their snouts and draw him to shore, defending him from other fish. When sailors wished to kill a certain lyre-player, Arion, he asked first to play his lyre. As he played, schools of dolphins gathered, and when he threw himself into the sea, one of them took him up and carried him safely to shore.

Others mourn a captured dolphin, as Pliny says, and bury a slain one. Under the emperor Augustus, a certain boy in Campania lured a dolphin with bread and eventually fed it by hand. At last he sat upon its back, and it often carried him out to sea and brought him back to shore. And when it found the boy, its companion in play, dead, it too died of grief before the eyes of many bystanders.

The river-horse [hippopotamus], as Aristotle says, is a monster of the eastern regions, of remarkable form, thriving equally on land and in water. It has a mane like a horse, cloven, hoof-like feet like a cow, and a lofty face. It has a tail like a pig, whinnies like a horse; its hide is very tough and thick, its inward parts like a horse's, and its size like that of a donkey.

The seal, the sea-ox, as the Experimentator says, is the strongest animal of its kind. It does not readily change its place, but always stays where nature first placed it. It is a spirited and irascible animal, though not toward other creatures, but toward its own household; for it always fights with its own mate, until it kills her. Once she is dead, it casts her out from its place and brings in another, and does not cease bringing in new mates this way, until it happens either to die its own death or to be overcome and killed by one of its mates. Its rival offspring live off this destruction as prey.

The swordfish is a monster of the sea, as Isidore and Pliny say, named from the thing itself, since it has a snout as sharp as a sword, with which it pierces and sinks ships. Its snout curves upward, its claws are cloven, its tail twisted, its teeth hooked and like those of a boar. It more readily takes wounds in its forequarters than in other parts of its body; spears are turned from its hide.

The 'kylion' is a quite remarkable sea animal, as Aristotle says, in which nature is believed to have erred, or to have reversed its usual order. For whereas in all land creatures, small and large alike, the liver is placed on the right and the spleen on the left, in the 'kylion,' however, nature has placed the spleen on the right and the liver on the left.

The 'ludolacra' is a sea animal of quite remarkable nature and form, as Aristotle says. It has four wings, arranged so: two on the front, two on the back, by which it drives itself with remarkable speed from place to place, wherever its will impels it.

'Sea monks' are sea monsters named from the thing itself. They have the shape of a fish in their lower parts, but in their upper parts, partly, a human appearance. They have a head shaped like the head of a freshly-shaven monk: a shaved, white crown on top, and a black ring around the head over the place of the ears, like the circle left by the hair on a monk's head, spaced widely apart. This monster gladly lures men walking along the seashore, and plays before them, and draws near with leaps. And if it sees a man taking delight in its play, it rejoices and plays all the more on the water's surface. But if it sees a man, drawn by wonder, drawing nearer, it too draws near, and, if given the chance, seizes the man and drags him into the depths, and so is sated on his flesh. Its face is not entirely like a man's, for it has a nose like a fish's, and its mouth continuous with its nose.
