Nereids are sea beasts. As Pliny says, they are shaggy and bristled over their whole body, and have another form fashioned like a man's. One of these, when, imitating the human condition, she must die, is heard from far off by those on the shore, moaning and lamenting, and confesses in her sorrow that the necessity of death is bitter for mortal creatures.

Sirens are noisy creatures, as Philosophus says, which from the head to the navel have the shape of a woman of tall stature, with a dreadful face and very long, matted hair on the head. They appear together with their offspring, whom they carry in their arms; for they suckle their young with breasts, which they have large on their chest.

The rest of their body, however, is like an eagle's, as Adelinus says, with claws on their feet fit for tearing; but at the end of their body they have scaly fish-tails, with which, like oars, they swim in the depths. They have a kind of musical and most sweet melody in their voice, by which sailors, delighted and drawn in, are dissolved into sleep, and are then torn apart by the sirens' claws. But sailors, using a prudent strategy, plug their ears tightly, so as not to be lured into sleep by the sirens' deadly song, until they have passed by. Sailors, too, when they see sirens, are greatly afraid, and then throw them empty flasks, with which they play, so that meanwhile the ship may pass. This is what those who have testified to having seen them report. Their song, however, should be believed not articulate, but indistinct in its notes, like the song of birds.

Scylla is a monster of the sea, hostile to sailors and to every man, and delights in their blood and flesh. Its head and chest are shaped like a maiden's, like the sirens'; it has a gaping, wide-open mouth with horrible teeth, a beast-like belly, and a tail like a dolphin's. As the Book of Nature says, they are of remarkable strength and are not easily overcome in the water; on land, however, they are weaker and nearly powerless.
Adelinus says: they also have somewhat musical voices, and take wondrous delight in flesh. Adelinus says this monster dwells in the sea that lies between Italy and Sicily.

Skinks, too, are frequently found near the Nile, as Isidore says, beasts indeed similar to crocodiles, but of a much smaller and narrower form. Cups tainted with their flesh neutralize the power of poison.

The 'testeum' is a monstrous sea animal; it may take its name from the thing itself, since it has a shell-like ['testeam'] skin. Aristotle: it is born in the Arabian Sea. When it falls ill, it seeks fresh water and drinks from it for some time; once healed, this animal returns to salt water. It is clear, moreover, that there is fresh water within the sea, and this can be proven thus: take a wax vessel, seal it on every side, and cast it, empty, into the sea for the space of a day and a night, and afterward you will find that same vessel full of fresh water.

No fish, as Aristotle says, has a neck, a penis, testicles, or breasts. From this, however, we exclude the sea monsters, since these breed after their own kind. Every fish, and every soft-shelled animal, sleeps little, and does not move except in its tail while sleeping, and even that only slightly.

[It is a sign that] fish withdraw when the region where they have been accustomed to remain is about to be laid waste. A fish is never seen to mate with fish of another kind, but each keeps its own natural order, both in sex and in kind.

Aristotle calls it the 'fastaleo.' Sea fish eat one another, except the creature Aristotle calls the 'fastaleo.' The reason for this is that this animal does not eat flesh at all. No sea creature eats its own young, except once they are fully grown and have taken on a form resembling their parents. The flesh of fish that dwell near the shores is stronger and more wholesome; the flesh of those that dwell in the depths is moister and less wholesome. All stone-eating fish are fat, and every shoal of fish has a leader. Every prey-hunting fish swims socially, like the pike and its kind. All fish that swim by their breadth, like the flatfish and the scallop, fatten when the south wind blows. Fish that are elongated, like the pike, are certainly fattened when the north wind blows. The females of fish are larger than the males. Fish are caught better before sunrise, since it is then that the sight of fish is most easily deceived. They see equally well by night as by day. They die from the taste of oil. The greater part of a fish's eggs perish when the female wanders about laying them. Some fish are generated by themselves without any mating, and some from the slime of other fish, some simply from earth, and some from putrefaction and decay, which appears to float on the water's surface like oil. Before the time of birth or mating they wander about. Certain fish, when they are breeding, grow weak, and for this reason are generally caught more at this time than at another. Drought harms fish, and most fish fatten in rainy weather, since rain benefits them just as it does plants of the earth. Hence they seem to swim up to the surface and play at the falling rain. If wood is rubbed with the liver of a sea fish, it appears to burn like oil too. Hence oil is customarily made from the livers of certain sea fish.

As the Experimentator says, certain fish will not touch the vessel used to catch them unless it is new. Female fish are longer than males and have tougher flesh. Fish always strive to return to the place of their birth, wherever they may have gone downstream or up, and for this reason they often meet with danger.
The great Basil says: see how each kind of fish has its own appointed region, and none encroaches on another's territory, but each is content with its own dwelling.

The eel is a fish like a serpent; hence it also takes its name from 'anguis' [snake]. The more tightly you grip it, the more quickly it slips away. It is skinned only with difficulty. Pliny: eels have neither a male nor a female sex.

Eels drowned in wine, as Isidore says, give those who drink of it a distaste for wine. Eel fat heals earache. It dies a very hard death, and lives on even when skinned. It is cooked longer than other fish; otherwise its meat is harmful. It is better roasted over a fire, since this evaporates its harmfulness. In the river Ganges there are eels thirty cubits in length.

Among all fish, the herring alone lives on water only and can only live in water. As soon as it comes into contact with clear air, it dies without delay. Its eyes shine at night in the sea like a light, but this power dies with the fish itself. Wherever they see a light over the water in the sea, they gather in shoals, and by this trick they are lured into nets. The best herrings are found around Scotland, the worst around Germany.

The sea too nourishes a golden fleece, as Ambrose attests, and the shores produce a wool the color of that celebrated metal. No one, however skilled in the art of covering fleeces with varied threads, has yet been able to imitate its color. It is believed that this was the very kind of fleece for which countless thousands of men were killed in the lands of the Trojans.
The 'aforus' is a tiny fish, as Isidore says, so small it cannot be caught by a hook. Apply this to the humility of the Blessed Virgin, for humility knows no fall.

The 'aranea' [weaver-fish] is a kind of sea fish, as Isidore says, which has stinging spines near the ear, and stings those who come near its ear. It signifies those who, having an itching ear for hearing evil reports about their neighbors, offer their ears to such tales and are wounded gravely thereby, and so: 'hedge your ears about with thorns!'

Flatfish are river fish that swim only by the breadth of their body; for they are very thin fish and very broad. They have fins all around the circumference of their broad body. When hunted by fishermen, they seek the bottom of the water and stir up the water above themselves, so as not to be seen, especially since, lying flat against the ground with their body, they look exactly like the ground above their back.

The whale is the largest of fish, as Isidore says. In its youth it has black teeth, which in any case turn white in old age. It has its mouth on its forehead. Some whales are so enormous that they look like islands, or forests, or mountains. These sometimes throw up sand on their backs. Sailors, under pressing need, sometimes land on these, rejoicing to have found land, so as to rest from the waves, and cast anchor and lower sail; and while they hope to rest, trusting in the false stability, they light fires. As soon as the beast senses these, suddenly and unexpectedly stirred, it dives down, and drags both ships and men down into the depths with it. And although it is the largest of all fish, it nonetheless has a narrow mouth-passage; hence it swallows only small fish, which it lures and draws to itself with the fragrant breath of its mouth and sends into its belly. When you see whales moving together, you would think a most swift torrent was flowing by, says Isidore. I myself have witnessed this and marveled at the wisdom of God. When the whale passes the age of three years, it mates with the female whale. Without delay, in that very act of mating, the strength of its genital member is impaired, so that it can never mate again, but, entering the deep sea, it grows so much that it can be caught by no human skill, so that, if you saw it, you would think mountains of infinite size rose from its towering peaks. It cannot, then, be caught before three years have passed; hearing the sound of pipes and musicians, it draws near.

Crabs have tough backs like crocodiles, and eight feet and arms together, with pincers in place of hands. It moves backward and never, as Adelinus says, knows how to walk facing forward. When they grow old, two white stones, tinged with a reddish hue, are found in their heads.

Some say these stones have such power that, given in a drink, they calm the stabbing pains of the heart, which is entirely credible, since, as Galen says in the Anatomy, the heart is most greatly strengthened by hard, stone-like substances, such as pearls, sapphires, hyacinths, and the like. Crabs are long-lived; the female's first leg is double, and simple on the sea side; the right arm is nearly always larger than all the others. Males have two spines between the belly and the tail, which females lack, and females instead have eggs in their belly. They are a remedy against serpent bites. A crab given milk to drink, without water, lives many days. From the belly, a crab's intestine extends all the way to the end of the tail. If it is black and full, this is a sign of goodness; but if it is empty and white, it is a sign of hunger, and then it is dangerous to eat them.

Shellfish and snails are so called because they hollow out — that is, empty — as the moon wanes; for the flesh of all closed sea creatures and shellfish, as Hrabanus says, swells as the moon waxes, and hollows out as it wanes. Pearl-bearing snails, as the same author says, seek the shores at night and conceive from the heavenly dew; hence pearls form in their flesh.

Solinus: shellfish grow lustful for conceiving at a certain time of year, and thirst for the dew as though for a husband, gaping open in desire of it, and when the moonlit rain is at its fullest, they drink in the longed-for dew with a kind of yawning, and so conceive and become pregnant. And according to the quality of that nourishing dew, the pearls take on their appearance; for if what they receive is clear, the little spheres become white; if it is cloudy, they either grow dull and pale, or become clouded with a reddish tinge, and so their birth comes more from the heavens than from the sea.

There is another kind of dolphin, but of smaller form, as Isidore says, called 'delfines,' which, when a storm approaches, play, appearing on the water's surface. By this sign sailors foretell an approaching storm.

They are so vigorous in the agility of their bodies that, on Solinus's testimony, they sometimes leap and fly clear over the sails of ships. They also approach fishermen, who cast at them an iron rake, which, rubbing against sandy skin, sinks into their flesh, and then the sea casts them up.

Sea-ravens [cormorants] are named from their cry, as Isidore says; for they grunt from the chest, and, betrayed by their own voice, are caught. They signify certain impatient people who, though they hide their impatience outwardly in their actions, nonetheless murmur inwardly in their hearts, and by this are often caught in the devil's snares.

The 'clautius,' also called the catfish ['glanis'], as Pliny says, turns away and bites at baited hooks without swallowing them, but instead ravages the bait, stripping it away. This fish signifies those who, although they avoid the outright vice of fornication, lest they be caught by the telltale sign of resulting offspring, are nonetheless most shamelessly stained by the circumstances surrounding fornication, such as kisses, illicit conversations, and the like.

The remora is a fish, as Isidore and Jacques say, half a foot long; it has such power that, by clinging on, it can hold back a ship. Though the winds rage, the storms rise, and the waves are lifted up, the ship nonetheless stands as though rooted, unmoving, unable either to go forward or to return, this little fish not so much holding it back as clinging to it.

Blessed Ambrose, Jacques of Acre, Aristotle, Isidore, and the great Basil agree on this. There is no other explanation for this astonishing wonder of the remora fish, except that God should be proclaimed wondrous in his creatures, and the folly of heretics confounded, who are willing to believe in nothing but the ordinary course of nature.

Sea-urchins belong to the crab family, as Pliny says, having spines in a similar way in place of feet. This fish cannot be eaten, since, eaten, it brings death to a man by dissolving the balance of his constitution. The sea-urchin, in the midst of the sea, gives a stability it cannot give to itself, but begs, as it were, from pebbles what it can abundantly grant to ships. They have their mouths in the middle of the body, almost glassy in appearance like a scorpion's; in place of teeth they have heavy spines in their mouth.

Their eggs are bitter, five in number, as Ambrose and Aristotle say. When the sea-urchin senses a coming storm, it clasps hold of a heavy stone, so as not to be dislodged by the waves; so tested, let it call on one of the saints.

The pike is a fish of the Danube; the sturgeon fish delights most of all in rubbing itself against the pike for sport. As soon as the pike notices this, it at once flees, and, fleeing, is followed by the sturgeon. Since both are large and cannot hide even in the strongest currents, thrashing about and churning the water ahead of themselves, they are often caught together. Once caught, given the strongest wine or milk to drink, once it is drunk on much wine, it can live for many days. It drinks four sextarii of wine before it becomes drunk. It has one intestine, few small bones, cartilaginous rather than solid; in the head, however, it has many solid ones. In this are signified those who in the affection of their heart have great intentions of virtue, but lack the effect of actually carrying them out.

The 'granus' is a sea fish. As Philosophus says, contrary to the nature of all other animals, it has a single eye at the top of its head. With this eye it always watches above, on guard against traps, and signifies the contemplative man who says: 'my eyes are ever toward the Lord.'

The flying-fish is a sea fish, as Pliny says, quite similar to the winged swallow. This fish, apart from the squid and one other sea fish, has a habit contrary to all other fish. For while it stays in the water like a fish, having wings, it rises up to the pleasant reaches of the upper air. These fish signify those who, though caught up for a time in worldly affairs by the duties of their office, nonetheless, when time and place allow, once they return to themselves and are mindful of the sweetness of heaven, rise up more eagerly to the contemplation of spiritual things.

The 'kalaoz' is a sea fish, as Aristotle says, of many forms. This fish, contrary to every other kind of fish, has this nature: that the rain of heaven, which usually helps other fish's life and fattening, is given to this fish as its ruin, because, if there is much rain, it is blinded, and consequently, since it cannot seek food, dies of hunger and starvation.

The pike is a fish, as the Book of Nature says, also called the 'water-wolf.' Its food is fish and whatever crawls in the manner of frogs. It devours a fish nearly its own size in this way: once it has overcome its prey, it devours the head first, and once that is digested, it adds the rest little by little, until it has consumed the whole. It spares no equal of its own kind, either out of natural cruelty, or because it is jealous of its food and impatient of any rival in plunder. Indeed it even pursues its own offspring, once they have taken on the form of fish.
They say that morays are of the female sex only, on Isidore's testimony, and conceive from a serpent.
For, as Basil reports, a viper calls it out of the water with a coaxing hiss, until it mates with it. Hence it is lured and caught by fishermen imitating the serpent's hiss.

Ambrose says that the serpent, before coming to the moray to mate with it, first vomits out all its venom. This signifies how great the kindness of a husband toward his wife ought to be, since they have come together in this, that they might be two in one flesh.

It is certain that a moray's [life] is in its tail, as Alexander says; for struck on the head it is scarcely killed, but struck on the tail, it dies at once. Morays have a venomous bite, but the bite is healed by the ash of their own head.

The sprat is a sea fish, as the Book of Nature says; it is two palms long. It seems worthless in the regions where it is caught, but carried to more distant places and salted, its scarcity makes it precious. Freshly caught and without salt, however, it makes a more delicate food for those who eat it. This fish signifies those who, though held cheap among their own people, since 'no prophet is accepted in his own country,' receive honors and high positions when they go among strangers.

Sprats, as Solinus says, along with shellfish, approach the shore at night and conceive pearls from the dew of heaven. When the shellfish receives the morning air's seed, the pearl becomes clearer; from the evening air's seed it becomes darker, and the more dew it has drunk in, the more the stone's size increases accordingly. If the shells are open and a flash of lightning suddenly strikes, they are shut tight by fear of the untimely disturbance. They swim in shoals, and whichever among them has the most experience leads the group.

The red mullet is a fish, as Isidore says, taking its name from the thing itself, since it is soft ['mollis'] and very tender. Eating it diminishes lust; it dulls the sharpness of the eyes, and those who often feed on it smell of fish.
Those killed by a red mullet develop a distaste for wine, as Hrabanus says.

Oysters, as Pliny says, are a kind of shellfish or snail, on whose flesh crabs live by a remarkable cunning. For when oysters sometimes open their shell, to glory in the pleasure of the milder air, a crab lays a sudden ambush for it and throws a stone between the oyster's shells, so that it cannot close them again, and, its closing thus prevented, gnaws away at the oyster's flesh.

The oyster ['ostrea'] is named from its shell ['testa'], whose inner softness nourishes the flesh. For the Greeks call the shell 'ostreum.' 'Ostrea' is neuter, but its flesh is referred to in the feminine.

The sea-pig is an edible fish; it largely resembles the shape of the land pig. Its tongue is free-moving, like a pig's, though they differ in voice. On its back there are certain spines with a most potent venom, but their gall is a remedy for the sting of those same spines. Their suffering, however, is great. As Pliny says, they seek food on the sea floor and root about there like pigs; they have their mouth-opening near the throat.

The sturgeon is a large fish in river waters; it takes in little or no food into its body, since the calm serenity of the air alone is sufficient nourishment for it; hence it happens that it has a small belly. It has intestines, although very small in proportion to its body, but a liver large enough, and so sweet that it can scarcely be eaten without the stomach's revulsion. Hence its gall, which lies beside it, is customarily rubbed into the liver, so that the excessive sweetness of the liver is tempered by the excessive bitterness of the gall. It has no mouth, and that part is whole which in other animals usually contains the mouth, and it has nothing but a small opening under its throat, which it closes at will, but opens to the clear air. When the south wind blows, it fattens more quickly, but when the north wind blows, it sinks into the depths. Placed in milk, it lives long without water.

Sea-centipedes, as Pliny says, resemble the land creatures called centipedes. When they swallow a hook, they expel all their inner organs, until they discharge the hook; then they draw them back in again. These fish signify those who, sensing earthly riches to be a danger to themselves, cast them off and vow themselves to the common life of a monastery. But when, having lingered there a while, they are unwilling to be content with the common allowance, they gather private property to themselves again, and become worse in this, returning like dogs to their vomit. They seek the depths, fleeing the sun's heat or hail, for these two things spoil their color. Placed in vinegar, they dissolve quickly. They are called 'uniones' [single pearls] because two are never found in one shell. A stone made from these, ground and prepared in the proper measure, is good against weakness of the stomach, has the power to promote harmony, and renders its bearer chaste.

The 'salpa' fish, as Pliny says, is an obscene and worthless fish. It can never be properly cooked unless it is first beaten vigorously with a stick or rod. This fish signifies certain sinners of sordid life, who can never be cooked by the fire of the Holy Spirit or of charity, so as to become a chosen dish of the divine will, unless they are first beneficially chastised by the lash of some sickness or tribulation.

The tortoise, as Isidore says, is named from being covered with a shell ['testa'] in the manner of a vaulted chamber. There are four kinds of tortoise: land tortoises, sea tortoises, shore tortoises — that is, those living in mud and marshes — and a fourth kind, river tortoises, which live in fresh water. Some report — though it is hard to believe — that ships carrying a tortoise's right foot sail more slowly.

The 'trebius' is a black fish, a foot long. Pliny reports that it has this power: a piece of it, kept in salt and brought near, draws up gold that has fallen into the deepest wells and makes it float.

Sea-vipers are fairly small sea fish, a little more than a cubit long; on their head, above the eyes, they bear a small horn, sharp and deadly. Whomever they wound with this same horn, they infect with poison. Guarding against this, fishermen, once they have caught the fish, cut off its head, and the rest of the body serves for human use, since it is quite edible.

We must look first, in general terms, at serpents. Aristotle: a serpent's tongue is thin, long, black, and forked, and so it seems to project a great deal from the mouth. Its heart lies behind the neck and resembles a kidney. Large serpents have their gall above the liver, small ones above the intestine. If a serpent is blinded, it regains its sight again, like the swallow; and if its tail is cut off, it grows back naturally, like small lizards. A serpent has thirty ribs. In mating, serpents join to one another so closely that they seem to be a single body with two heads. Every serpent eats flesh and plants without distinction. It is an animal of scanty drink. A serpent greatly desires wine; hence those who hunt them lure them with wine.

The earth, once a man has been killed by a serpent, as Pliny says, no longer receives it, but the serpent pays the penalty, doomed to die shortly after. A serpent can kill only one victim, no more, except the salamander alone. Venom, as Pliny says, is nothing other than the gall of serpents, which travels from there to the veins beneath the spine and afterward reaches the mouth, or the tail, as in scorpions. In Syria there are snakes that do no harm; for this reason the Syrians do not kill them.

Aristotle says that in Lacedaemon, on Mount Caria, foreign visitors are not harmed by scorpions, though they kill the natives. Serpents are by nature hot creatures, and so they do little or no harm once they have grown cold; they harm less by night than by day, since they are chilled by the night dew. Those killed by venom first grow stiff; but once the venom has become heated, it kills a man through dryness. It is said that a serpent cannot do harm unless it happens to touch human blood. It is also said that a serpent flees from a naked man and does not dare molest him.

Ambrose: the spittle of a fasting man kills a serpent; for if a serpent is touched by even a little of it, it dies at once. See, O man, how great is the power of fasting, that it can kill an earthly serpent with its spittle, and, deservedly, the spiritual one too. There are as many venoms as there are kinds of serpents, as many destructions as species, as many pains as colors. Its spleen is small and round. A serpent, hiding its head, exposes its whole body to the one striking it; for if it saves its head, it will live even having lost its body. About to enter water, it lays aside its venoms, and once it leaves the water, it takes them up again. And if, by whatever chance, it should fail to find its lost venoms again, it will often dash its head against the ground and die of grief. It flees a pleasant scent, and is often killed by that very means. Serpents are said to be generated from human marrow, especially from the spine.

Hrabanus: 'venenum' [venom] is so called because it travels through the veins ['venas']; for it cannot do harm until it has touched the blood. All venom, moreover, is cold, and so the soul, being fiery, flees from venom.
Aristotle: it is proper to the serpent that it can move its head while its body remains still.
Hrabanus: all snakes have dull sight; hence they rarely look straight ahead. For they have their eyes not in the forehead but at the temples, so that they hear more quickly than they see.
Alexander: the serpent expels the blindness caused by fennel. And so, when it senses its eyes clouding over, it seeks out this known remedy, and is not disappointed of its effect.
Aristotle: no animal moves its tongue with such speed, so that it seems to have a threefold tongue, though it has but one.
Augustine: venom is death to man, life to the serpent.

Isidore: the bodies of serpents are so bare that wherever they go they mark the path with moisture. Their tracks are such that, although they seem to lack feet, they nonetheless crawl using their ribs and the action of their scales. For they support themselves on their scales as though on claws, and on their ribs as though on legs. These scales, indeed, they have arranged evenly from the top of the throat down to the bottom of the belly.

The asp is a serpent of sky-blue color; by its bite it injects and spreads venom, from which it also takes its name. For 'aspis' means 'venom' in Greek, as Jacques says. The asp is charmed by the power of certain words, so as not to harm with its venom, or, as some say, so that, once stilled, it may be caught and the precious stone that naturally grows in its forehead removed; but it is naturally wary against enchantment. For it presses one ear to the ground and blocks the other with its tail, so as not to hear the enchanter's voice, cleverly.
Lucan calls it the 'sleep-bringer,' because whoever is wounded by it passes into a sleep that continues into death.

As Solinus says, the asp lives only with a mate, and from this it happens that, when one is killed, the other, unbelievably, pursues the killer for the sake of vengeance and, however large the company he travels in, harasses him relentlessly; it breaks through every obstacle and crosses vast distances, and, unless a river bars its way or the man escapes with utmost speed, it does not let the killer of its mate live.

As the Experimentator says, the asp does no harm to Africans or Syrians; hence they cast their own newborn children before serpents. If the serpents harm them, they cast them away as illegitimate; but if not, they raise them as their own.

The 'amphisbaena' is a serpent with two heads, one in its usual place, the other on its tail. This is the cause of the serpent's ability to move in circling paths with either head leading. Solinus calls this creature the 'amphis' in his book, and Aristotle also reports of eastern serpents that have two heads. But he says this comes from a monstrous birth; for they have two heads and one body. Both heads take in food and pass it into the single body, and both heads move forward against attackers.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie; De animalibus Iorath

cit.quote: Juba, in his book On Animals, says that the amphisbaena keeps such careful watch while brooding her eggs that, while one part of her sleeps, the other keeps watch.

The basilisk, as Jacques says, is a serpent said to be the king of serpents; hence 'basiliscus' in Greek is the same as 'regulus' [little king] in Latin. The basilisk is a singular evil upon the earth, half a foot long, marked on the head with white spots as though bearing a kind of diadem. All serpents fear and flee it, since it kills them by its breath alone, while it kills men by its venomous gaze alone. For if it sees a man first, the man dies; but if the man sees the serpent first, the serpent dies, as Jacques of Acre says. No bird passes unharmed within sight of it; it pollutes the ground it crosses and withers the grass, poisons trees, kills shrubs, and corrupts the air so much that no bird flies through the infected air unharmed.

No bird passes unharmed within sight of the basilisk. Whatever comes near its mouth is scorched and consumed. It infects the air with a pestilent breath. At its mere breath it splits rocks apart. When it moves, it slithers with the middle part of its body, while the rest is held upright and raised. Whatever it kills with its bite is eaten neither by beast nor bird. Even other serpents dread its hiss. It is also called by that name because it kills by hissing ['sibilus']. It is overcome by the weasel, however, which men introduce into the caverns where it lurks.

Once the basilisks are killed, as Pliny says, the weasels die too. Yet its power does not leave it even when it is dead. For wherever its ash has been smeared, spiders cannot spin their webs, nor can any venomous creature be touched, nor birds foul the place. This is also said to occur in whatever house a part of its body is kept. Silver, it is said, smeared with its ash, takes on the color of gold. There is a certain kind of basilisk that flies, but it does not go beyond the boundaries of its own region, which divine order has set for it, lest it turn to cover the whole earth. There is another kind of basilisk, according to the writings of the ancients, which is generated from an egg laid by a decrepit, aging cock.

The 'boa' is a snake found in Calabria, as Solinus says, which grows to an immense size in this way: it first attacks buffaloes or cows, and, whichever are flowing with an abundance of milk, attaches itself to their udders and sucks. Continually gorged and nourished this way over a long span of time, it eventually grows, through such gluttony, so large that no strength can resist its size, and finally, once it has laid waste the regions it has invaded, it forces the land into ruin.
Hence Jerome writes: blessed Hilarion, when asked, by the power of the divine word compelled it to climb a pile of firewood, and, once the pyre was set alight, burned up the monstrous beast.

A certain kind of dragon can swallow whole stags and oxen. Of this kind is believed to have been the snake that Regulus, the Roman commander, as the Roman History itself records, killed in Africa, a hundred and twenty feet long, whose skin, once stripped, was carried to Rome as a spectacle, and whose jawbones too were hung up at Rome as a wonder. Pliny writes of this serpent that, when it was being captured, it was necessary to bring in siege engines and various war machines, as in the storming of a fortress.

The viper is the most wicked kind of serpent, as the Experimentator says, and craftier than all other serpents. This serpent calls the moray eel to the shore with a hiss and coaxes it, so as to entice it into mating. But the sea-moray is soft-hearted, and submits to the mating, though sometimes to its own destruction. For, killed by the ambush of its enemies before it can return to the water, it is killed and pays the price for its own destruction. Apply this to women who are led out of their homes by the hissing sound of pipes and lyres by young men, and, corrupted by the devil, are killed in soul.

The horned viper is a serpent, as Solinus says, having nine horns on its head resembling a ram's. It hides its whole body in the sand, leaving only the horns exposed. When sparrows or other birds land on these to rest, the venomous serpent seizes and devours the slain. This serpent, moreover, is more flexible than other serpents, and this because it does not appear to have a spine to stiffen it. Its horn, placed on the tables of the wealthy, reveals venom by sweating. Knife-handles are made from these horns; such knives were placed on the tables of emperors before every meal, so that they might reveal by sweating whether any food that had been served was tainted with poison.

The horned viper is so named because it has horns on its head resembling a ram's; for the Greeks call horns 'cerata.' It has four small horns, by whose display, as though by bait, it lures curious animals and kills them.

The 'chelydrus' is a serpent, as Isidore says, that dwells both in water and on land. It gets its name from the thing itself; for 'chyron' in Greek means land, and 'hydros' water. It makes the ground it crosses smoke. It always moves in a straight line; for if it twists itself while moving, it immediately splits open.
The 'cenchris' is a straight-moving serpent, as Isidore says, which always travels a direct path.
Hence Lucan: 'and the cenchris, ever gliding on a straight track.'
But the centipede is a serpent with many feet, as Isidore says.

Against the three kinds of serpents, as Jacques says, that afflicted the children of Israel in the wilderness, a bronze serpent was set up on a pole by Moses, at the command of the Lord. These, they say, were the 'dipsas,' the 'situla,' and the scorpion.

The 'dipsas' is a serpent, as Jacques and Solinus say, said to be so slight that its bite, delivered almost invisibly, cannot be seen when it strikes. It kills, on Solinus's testimony, by thirst; for it induces through this a swelling and inflation, and so, infected by the venom, one dies — and it signifies pride.

As the Experimentator says, the 'dipsas' kills in such a way that death overtakes the face before it can put on the sadness of one dying. The proud are indeed crushed only with difficulty, as is plain in the devil, who is damned by pride alone; for he never deigns to seek pardon by confessing himself guilty of his crime.

The dragon is the largest of all creatures on earth, as Jacques and Augustine say. It has no venom, but is crested on the head, and has a mouth small in proportion to the size of its body, and narrow windpipes. It puts out its tongue toward its throat and gapes its mouth, but does no harm with its teeth.

Its bite, however, is exceedingly bad even though small, as the Experimentator says, since it eats venomous things; but if it binds someone with its tail, it kills him. Not even the elephant is safe from it, for all the size of its body.

In springtime the dragon suffers nausea, which it relieves with the juice of lettuce, as Pliny says. Its dwelling is most often in caves, which it readily chooses in stony cliffs, because of the excessive inward heat of its own nature — this especially when it has been flying — and because of the accidental heat of the sun, which is greatest in those regions, namely of the East. Its voice and roaring terrify men. Its sight is unbearable to men, so much so that they are sometimes frightened to death by the mere sight of it.
Reaching old age and its full growth, it lives a long time without food, as Aristotle says; but once it has eaten, it is not easily satisfied.

The dragon sometimes dwells in the depths of the earth, as Augustine says, and, when it senses a storm in the air, comes out and is borne aloft over the air with great strokes of its wings, stirring and driving the air with wings made of a leathery, pliant substance, and spread widely in proportion to the size of its body. Wherever it dwells, it poisons the air, breathing a deadly breath that spreads plague. It lacks feet; a certain kind of them crawls on the ground on its belly. There is another kind that has feet; this kind is rarer.

From its brain a stone called 'draguncia' is cut out, as Adelinus says, but they say it is never precious unless extracted while the creature is alive. For, unexpectedly, with a single blow, dragons lying in the heat are struck through the head, and so, while they still tremble in full vigor, the stone is extracted. A dragon's tongue and gall, boiled in wine, are a remedy for those tormented by demons, once their bodies are anointed with it. Dragon flesh is glassy in color and cools those who eat it. Hence it is that the Ethiopians, in that scorching climate, gladly eat dragon flesh, since it is exceedingly cold. The dragon grows very hot in flight, and then desires to be refreshed with elephant blood, which is indeed the coldest in its effect. It fears the crash of thunder and lightning above all other animals, and so, when it hears thunder, it flees into caves and hollows of the earth.

No wonder, for it is said that, among all animals, the dragon's nature is struck by lightning more readily than any other, as it is written on Pliny's testimony. By contrast, the eagle among birds and the laurel among trees are never struck by lightning. A dragon can grow to twenty cubits or more, so much so that it can carry its rider over great stretches of land, but, once wearied, plunges itself and its rider into the sea. It is struck with rods of coral before a wineskin filled with air; fearing this sound, it yields and becomes obedient.

The 'dracontopedes' are serpents, and, as Adelinus reports, the Greeks call them great and powerful. They have maidens' faces resembling human faces, but end below in a dragon's body. Of this kind of serpent it may be believed was the serpent by which Eve was deceived.

For Bede says that that serpent had a maiden's face, so that the devil might entice her by a similarly attractive form; for every animal loves what resembles itself. The rest of its body, resembling a serpent, it hid among the fruits of the trees. How the devil could have made the serpent form articulate words, however, we cannot see, unless perhaps we wish to say that, just as the serpent had a human face, so too it had the throat and organs arranged to produce human speech if taught, just as birds imitate human voices by speaking.

The 'haemorrhois,' as Isidore says, is a serpent so named because whoever is bitten by it sweats blood, so that, its veins loosened, it draws out through the blood whatever life remains. For 'haima' means blood in Greek.

[The serpent 'ipnale'] is a serpent, as Solinus says, of the asp family, which kills those it bites through sleep. For it induces sleep through its venom, which, once instilled, leaves the victim without any further struggle. This is the serpent that Cleopatra took hold of, placing it against her left arm as she lay in the tomb beside her husband Antony, so that, by its touch, she might dissolve into sleep and end her life in a peaceful death. Solinus calls it 'ipsinale'; Jerome and the Roman History, however, call it an asp, since this 'ipsinale' is indeed a kind of asp.

The 'hydros,' as Isidore says, is a serpent in the river Nile. When it sees a crocodile with its mouth open on the banks of the Nile, it rolls itself in muddy slime, so that it can more easily slip into the crocodile's jaws. The drowsy crocodile then swallows it as it slips in, and soon, once its innards are torn apart, the hydros emerges alive.

Among snakes, as Pliny says, the hydros is the most beautiful in the world; its liver is kept as a remedy for those bitten. Men struck by this serpent swell up; this disease they call 'boa,' because it is cured with cattle dung.

The hydra, as Isidore says, is a dragon of many heads, such as lived in the Lernaean marsh of the province of Arcadia. It is called 'excedra' in Latin, because, for each head cut off, three grew back. But this is fabulous; for it is well established that the Hydra was a place spewing forth waters and laying waste a neighboring city, in which, when one channel was blocked, many others would burst forth; seeing this, Hercules burned and dried out those very places and blocked those channels. For 'Hydra' takes its name from water.
The 'iaculus' is a flying serpent, as Isidore says.
'the flying iaculi.'
For they leap up into trees, and when some animal happens to pass beneath them, they hurl themselves down upon it and kill it, whence they are also called 'iaculi' [javelin-serpents].

The lizard, as Solinus says, is called by the ancients a worm rather than a serpent, since it is milder in its ferocity; it hisses like a serpent, however, and has a similar tail. It has a forked, hairy tongue; it feeds on wild spiders.

The lizard, as Pliny says, never forgets the place where she gave birth, since she has no memory at all otherwise. Her young burst forth by themselves, eleven in number. Some say that the young are devoured by their mothers, except one, the cleverest, which is left and preys on its own mother's flesh. This one, left behind, avenges its siblings and kills its own parent as their avenger. In India there are lizards twenty-four feet long, of a shining color.
The water-snake, as Isidore says, poisons water with its venom; for in whatever spring it dwells, it mixes its venom into it.
Hence Lucan: 'and the water-snake, defiler of the water.'

The 'naderos' is a snake found in the regions of Germany, about the thickness of a human arm, golden in color and belly, with a green back. Its breath is said to be so harmful that, if a freshly cut rod is held to its mouth, its breath makes the bark bubble up into gall-like blisters. And if you hold a bright sword to its mouth, its tongue alone, touching the sword at the base, poisons it, and the venom runs up to the top of the sword, staining it a sky-blue color, as though corrupted by a violent flame. A man infected by this venom dies, unless treacle is applied to help him. The nature of this venom is such that, once it has struck a man in the foot, the venom runs by degrees to the other limbs, and this through the excessive intensity of its heat. It has the same nature as fire, which always rises. So then, the venom always rises, until it reaches the heart, and then the man falls down and dies. There is, however, a remedy: that a man struck in the foot be hung upside-down by the feet, head lowered, and so the venom cannot reach the heart, but stops upon reaching the top of the foot, and so the infected place is cut out and healed with medicines. If anyone wishes to walk safely, that is, securely, in a place where these serpents dwell, let him rub his feet and hands and other exposed limbs with rue and wormwood, and so he will always escape them, since the serpents will not dare touch limbs anointed with the remedies of these herbs.
The 'parias,' as Isidore says, is a serpent that always moves along on its tail and seems to make a furrow as it goes.
Of which Lucan says: 'content to furrow its path with its tail, the parias.'

[The 'pareas'] is a serpent, as Jacques and Solinus say, that always moves with its mouth open and steaming. Whomever it strikes, it swells to an enormous bulk, as though afflicted with dropsy, and so dies.

The 'rutela' is a serpent of the East, created usefully for many remedies, as Aristotle says. This kind of serpent is caught by apothecaries and kept in captivity. In it, note that it lives a long time without any nourishment of food at all; indeed every kind of serpent can live a long time without food, but the 'rutela' especially so.
The salamander, as Jacques says, is called 'stellio' in Greek.
Some call it 'chamaeleon,' that is, 'earth-lion,' as Pliny and Adelinus say.
It is, they say, four-footed, with a face like a lizard's, or, as Aristotle says, a face somewhere between that of a pig and an ape.

Its legs are straight behind and rather long, held close to the belly; its tail is long and twisting, tapering to a fine point. Its claws are hooked, delicately curved; its body has a rough skin, like that of a crocodile.
It lives in fire, and not only is not burned, but even extinguishes the blaze, as Augustine, Adelinus, and Isidore say.

Its gait is sluggish, as Solinus says, almost like the movement of tortoises; its eyes are set back in a hollow recess, and never close, and Pliny says its eyes can turn all the way around. Its liver lies on the left side, contrary to all other animals.

The gape of its mouth is never closed, since it does not use it for the purpose of food or drink, because it lives only on the sipping of dew or air, as Aristotle says. It is very lean, and the reason is that it has little blood, and so it is a fearful animal, since the heat that spurs boldness is diminished in it.

The fear of this animal, moreover, is the cause of its color being varied and changeable by the moment, so that it takes on the color of whatever it touches, as Ambrose says. There are two colors, however, it cannot take on: white and red. Its body is almost without flesh, and only the tiniest amount of blood is found in its heart. It has no spleen. In winter it hides, and appears again in spring.

Among all venomous animals, as Isidore says, the salamander has the greatest power to harm. If a salamander crawls up a tree, it poisons its fruit, so that whoever eats of it dies. And if it falls into a well, the power of its venom kills those who drink from it. There is a very great abundance of these creatures in Asia. The salamander has neither male nor female, but all lay eggs, wherever they wish, in the manner of hens, and produce their young from these. It is reported that Pope Alexander had a garment woven from the wool of this animal, which, whenever it needed to be cleaned, was washed with no other water than being thrown into the fire, where it grew white-hot in the flames. I myself have also seen a belt woven from this animal's wool, which, to test the truth of it, I threw with my own hand into a roaring fire, and, taking it out again after a long space of time, glowing like iron from the fire, and, once it had cooled after an hour, I handled it with my own hands and could not find that even a single hair of it had been consumed. Isidore too reports that a certain belt woven of this kind of wool could not be burned.

The 'salpiga' is a serpent not easily seen because of its smallness, and yet it has the greatest power to do harm. Apply this to hidden rancor in the heart, which does much harm, though it is not easily recognized.

The 'stellio,' as Isidore says, takes its name from its color; for its back is marked with shining spots like little stars. It is so opposed to scorpions that its very sight brings them dread and paralysis. It signifies those who, endowed with the beauty of natural goodness or with the strength of heavenly grace, are a terror to those who do evil.

The 'stellio' is a serpent, as Pliny says. Its venom is deadly, but a remedy against it is made from the crushed flesh of a scorpion. Wine in which a 'stellio' has drowned and died causes freckles on the face. The gall of the 'stellio,' crushed in water, is said to gather weasels by some hidden instinct. The 'stellio' is greatly opposed to scorpions, and they pursue each other with natural hatred; but since the 'stellio' is larger and stronger, the scorpion fears it remarkably, so much so that at the sight of it it breaks out in a cold sweat.

The 'scaura' is a serpent; when it grows old, its eyes go blind, as Jacques and Solinus say; it then enters an opening in a wall facing the sunrise, so that, when the sun rises, it may fix its eyes toward the sun and so recover its sight.
The 'sibilus,' as Isidore says, is the same as the 'regulus' serpent; for it kills by hissing, before it bites or scorches.
[The serpent 'spectaficus'] is a serpent, as Isidore says, that, once it has bitten a man, immediately consumes him, so that he dissolves entirely inside the serpent's mouth.

The 'scytale' is a serpent, as Isidore says, so called because it gleams with such variety on its back that it delays onlookers, admiring its markings; and because it is rather sluggish in crawling, it catches those it cannot otherwise overtake by astonishing them with this marvel.

The common serpent, as Alexander says, gives a sleeping man a reprieve, but once the man wakes, he is struck by the serpent. Apply this against those who strike at someone absent, who, as though asleep, neither hears, nor sees, nor feels it.

The 'situla,' as Jacques and Solinus say, is a small, malicious serpent, which kills a man through thirst. This serpent gleams with such variety that it delays onlookers by its beauty, and, though nature made it rather sluggish in crawling, it detains, astonished by its marvel, those it cannot otherwise overtake. It is, moreover, of such heat that it sheds its skin in winter. If someone is touched by its bite, he is seized by a burning heat and is set alight and consumed.

'Syrenes' are serpents, just as sirens are sea monsters. As the Experimentator says, they dwell in the regions of Arabia and are stronger in speed than horses. Some of them have wings and can fly. Their venom is so effective in bringing death that death follows the bite before the pain does.

The scorpion is a serpent, as Solinus says, said to have a gentle, almost maidenly face, but it has, in any case, a venomous sting in its knotted tail, with which it stings and poisons whoever draws near. It strikes with a sideways, curving blow, and never for a moment stops seeking opportunities to strike. Those infected by its venom draw out their death over three days. It is reported that some have twin stingers, and that the males are fiercer; these are recognized by their slenderness and length. For a man who has been stung by a scorpion, the ash of the scorpion itself, drunk in wine, is thought to be a remedy.

The scorpion lives on land, as the Experimentator says. Aristotle: the scorpion has two stingers, and when it bites black pigs, it kills them, and more quickly if they then enter water at once; a pig of another color, however, escapes, though not always. It is proper to the scorpion that it does not sting the palm of the hand, and touches nothing that is not hairy. For the oil made from scorpions is a remedy for their own bites. If you submerge a scorpion in oil and then pour vinegar over it, it revives at once under the sun; for oil blocks the pores, while vinegar opens them.
The scorpion, as Jerome says, strikes with an arched wound, that is, a triangular one.
The 'serps,' as Solinus says, is a serpent small in body but immense in malice. If it strikes, it consumes flesh and bone together with its venom, as though seized by a devouring flame.

Some hold that the tortoise belongs to the serpent family. It is an animal with two feet; it is covered by two very hard shields as though by a shell, and so armored that it can scarcely be killed even by the strongest blows. It has a head like a toad's, a tail like a scorpion's, and a feeble voice. It lays eggs like a hen, but its eggs are harmful to eat. It lacks venom in life, but by no means after death. For as Ambrose says, if someone treads with a bare foot on its kidneys after death, he is at once infected with venom.

The female tortoise, as Aristotle says, has only one passage for the discharge of waste, although it has a bladder. It therefore has a bladder, contrary to the nature of all animals that have feathers, scales, or a shell, since all these lack a bladder.

The 'tarans' is a serpent, as Pliny says, of the scorpion family. It is small, has wings, is capable of flight, and is dangerous; for whomever it stings dies, unless treacle or other medical remedies come to his aid. Italy has many of these, but often harmless ones; the East, however, has many, but they are always venomous. It generally lives twenty days or more without food. Once killed and left to putrefy in oil, that very oil becomes a remedy against poison and against the tarans's stings.

The 'tysus' is a serpent found in the Paduan mountains, six or seven feet long, though very slender, and thicker in its hindquarters than in its forequarters. It harms no one, unless gravely provoked. Its flesh, left to putrefy and then given as food and drink, is used against leprosy and is often a most effective remedy.

The 'tyrus,' as Jacques and the Book of Nature say, is a serpent found in the region of Jericho facing the wilderness of the Jordan. This serpent is hostile to birds and animals, and especially to the eggs of birds, which it eats and swallows along with the eggs themselves. Its flesh, prepared like an electuary with certain other ingredients mixed in, roots out poison. This preparation is called 'theriac.' Some report that before the Passion of Christ there was no remedy for this serpent's bite, and that it was especially hostile to men. It is said to have happened that, on the very day Christ was hung upon the cross, one of the most dangerous of these serpents, caught near Jerusalem, was hung on the cross beside Christ's own side, and that from that day this whole kind of serpent received, through the shedding of Christ's blood, the power to become a most effective remedy against every poison. But while theriac is effective against every poison, it is of no use against the venom of the 'tyrus' itself, which is called 'tychicon.'

The viper, as Jacques and Isidore say, is a serpent so named because it gives birth by force ['vi pariat']. Its nature is reported to be such that the father dies at the moment of conception, and the mother is killed in giving birth. For in the pleasure of mating, the female, driven as though to madness, clamps down on the male's head, taken into her mouth, and severs it. And when her belly, coming to term, has swollen, the young, not awaiting the mature loosening of nature, gnaw through her sides and burst forth by force, killing their mother. They have only cavities in place of ears, and only three teeth. Its bite is said to be beyond remedy; it also causes swelling and inflammation. This indeed was known to those who escaped the sea with Paul, and who, when a viper attacked Paul's hand, believed he would swell up and suddenly fall down dead.
The internal organs of all serpents are the target of the bite, as Pliny says [text incomplete].
The Experimentator says that a viper's cast-off skin, that is, the covering it sheds when it renews itself, boiled in wine, heals the teeth and eyes. Its fat, however, removes clouding of the eyes.
The Physiologus says that the viper has a human face down to the navel, but from the navel to the tail, the shape of a crocodile.

Its digestive passage is said to be like the eye of a needle, and for this reason it cannot conceive in the manner of other beasts, but only through the mouth — though Pliny seems to speak much more truly and credibly on this, being deeper in his reasoning. For he says of the viper that the pregnant mother, coming to the time of birth, expels one young each day, and, since there come to be many offspring, as many as twenty, the rest, which cannot be expelled and remain past the proper time, growing impatient with the delay, burst through her sides, killing their mother.

This serpent, though it is nearly the cruelest of all kinds of serpents, is nonetheless gentle toward its own mate, as the great Basil and Ambrose say. For the viper, when its mate is absent, seeks her out, calls to the absent one, and cries out with a coaxing hiss, and, when it senses its mate drawing near, vomits out its venom, showing reverence to its wife and holding the grace of marriage in respect and honor. And you, then, O man, endowed with reason, repudiate your own wife and think her to be exchanged often, and, if she is absent for a single day, you suspect her of adultery, and soon, the matter still unknown, you pursue a wrong as though it were established fact! Set aside your harshness, when your devoted wife comes to meet you; drive away your indignation! For you are not a master, but a husband; you have not taken a handmaid by lot, but a wife.

We must look first, in general terms, at worms. Isidore: a worm is an animal generally born from flesh, or wood, or any earthly matter whatsoever, without any mating, although it is sometimes born from eggs, as the scorpion is.

None of the 'infecta' [insects and creeping things], that is, worms, as Pliny says, has blood, except in a very small quantity. 'Infecta' is the name given to every kind of breeding worm. Some worms have no feet, yet have bones inside like serpents; these crawl along the ground. Others have no bones at all in their body and no feet, and these instead draw themselves along by means of very fine wrinkle-like folds stretched across their skin, by which they move or creep. Others, which have two feet or four, run, and have some small amount of blood. Others still, which have more than four feet, also run, but are entirely without blood, and this because the blood, as it passes into the nourishment of the many feet, is used up entirely. Every kind of worm has a fluid resembling blood in place of true blood.

Bees, as Aristotle, the great Basil, and Ambrose report, have, among all kinds of living creatures, a shared offspring; they all dwell in a single home, are enclosed within the bounds of a single homeland, share labor in common, common food, common work, common use and enjoyment, common flight. What more? Common to all of them is their manner of generation and the virginal wholeness of their bodies, and common to all of them too is their giving birth, since they are never joined to one another by any mating, nor are they undone by lust, nor shaken by the pains of childbirth, and yet all at once they send forth a vast swarm of offspring. They appoint their own king, create their own peoples, and, although set under a king, remain free. For they retain the privilege of judgment and the devotion of loyal affection, since they love him as though appointed by themselves, and honor him with such unanimity that no controversy or discord is ever stirred up against him. No wonder, since the king's sure devotion to his people, and the people's obedience to their king, are both preserved. Bees hold private council and fly in swarms to their leaders. They harm no crops, not even dead flowers. Caught out at night on an expedition, they keep watch lying on their backs, so as to protect their wings from dew and rain. The people of bees are divided into three groups. There are kings and, as it were, princes among bees; for in one hive only one rules with the marks of imperial authority. This one is more outstanding in form and twice as large as the rest, its wings shorter, its legs upright, its gait more lofty, with a certain mark on its forehead, white as though wearing a kind of diadem; it also differs from the common bees by a much greater sheen. The emperor of the bees has no sting, being armed with majesty alone. The first group of bees, then, consists of those that are mothers and past their prime, and are of lesser standing than the rest. The second group is the younger bees, who, performing their work with great vigor, are subject to the mothers as though by a kind of discipline, and do nothing without the elders' command. The third group of bees is called the drones. These are without a sting, like imperfect bees; they are, as it were, retainers and servants of the first and true bees. They accompany their young emperor with attentive reverence. They lay out the work of their dwelling in the manner of a military camp: the first roughly three rows are built empty, so that nothing readily invites one standing outside; the last rows are filled most fully with honey. They rest in the morning, until one rouses them with a double or triple trumpet call. If the coming day is to be mild — for they foreknow rain and wind — then they all fly forth together; but if it is to be stormy, they stay under cover. So then, when the company sets out to work, some gather flowers with their feet, others gather drops of water in their mouths and on the down of their whole body. Ambrose: you see them all vying over their task, some keeping watch to seek provisions, some anxiously guarding the camp, others foretelling coming rains and observing the courses of the stars. Whichever are in their youth go out to work and carry in what has been described above; the older ones work inside. Those that carry in flowers load their thighs with their front legs, and return entirely laden, the burden hanging heavy. Inside there are divided duties: some build, some polish, some bring supplies, others distribute the food from what has been brought in. Nor do they eat apart from one another, so that no inequality of work, food, or time arises among them.

Pliny: a wondrous discipline of work: they note the idleness of those who slack off, reprove them at once, and punish them with death. A wondrous cleanliness among them: all waste is gathered together in the middle; no filth lies scattered among their tasks, since they even deposit the workers' own excrement inside, so that they need not travel far, in order to carry it out, gathered together in one place, on stormy days or during a lull in their labor. As evening falls, they buzz less and less within the hive, until one flies around, ordering rest with the same trumpet call by which she roused them, in the manner of a military camp. Then all at once fall silent. They build homes first for the common people, then for their kings. If a more abundant yield is expected, they add more chambers. They construct palaces for their future emperors on one side of the hive, spacious, magnificent, set apart, and rising above the rest. The king is not chosen by lot, but is the one who excels in size and appearance of body, and also in gentleness of disposition.

Though it has a sting, it does not use it for vengeance, as Ambrose says. If the bees do not obey the laws of their king, they condemn themselves to death with the wound of their own sting, which the Persian peoples too are said to observe even today. Nor do they go out to any pasture unless the king has gone out first, and claims the leadership of the flight for himself. They defend their king with the greatest protection, and think it a fine thing to die for him.

Aristotle: kings never appear outside the hive alone, but only with a great escort of bees, and the king himself is in the middle, with the bees all around. If someone passing by offends against the wing of the emperor's guard, he will not escape the swarm. When they go out, each one wishes to be nearest to him and rejoices to be seen at his service. They lift up the weary on their shoulders, and the stronger ones carry them the whole way.

When their honey stores run low, as Pliny says, they make an attack and rush upon their neighbors with plundering intent; but the others draw up their ranks in resistance. They also fight for other reasons, namely over the carrying of flowers. Such fighting is entirely broken up by throwing dust or by smoke, but they are reconciled with milk or water. They hate foul odors and flee far from them. Even artificial perfumes trouble them.

Basil: in bees and wasps, segments appear all over the body, since in these creatures there is no breathing and no lung, but they are nourished entirely, throughout their whole body, by the air; and for this reason, when oil is poured on them, they perish, their pores blocked, but when vinegar is applied at once, they revive, their pores reopened. When bees fall ill, they eat more than usual, and they do this only out of the devotion they hold toward honey. They have an enemy in the moth, and not in one way only; for it feeds on the wax and leaves behind excrement from which wood-boring worms are generated. Frogs also lie in wait for them as they go to water, and frogs are said not to feel the sting of bees. Wasps and hornets, too, naturally attack them; swallows and other birds prey upon them. Bees accompany funerals in the manner of mourners. When their emperor is carried off by disease, the whole people grieves. These are the true signs of their sorrow: they do not gather food, nor do they go forth, but gather sadly around their emperor's body, and, watching the swarm, they mourn.

Then, unless they are helped, they die of hunger, as the Experimentator says. Bees fall ill especially when the flowers grow cold. An echo, with its resounding sound, is their enemy, and so are clouds of mist. Spiders too are especially hostile to them; once they gain the upper hand and have woven their webs, they kill them.

Their own good fortune harms bees; for if the year is too abundant in flowers, while they occupy themselves solely with the work of making honey, they give no thought to breeding. Bees die from many causes, and especially if there are too many rulers, and each one governs a single faction. They delight in applause and the ringing of bronze, and are called together by it. Bees can be produced from the fresh entrails of buffaloes buried in dung. Likewise, bees are born from bull's hide buried in the ground, wasps from donkey's hide, mint-flies from the dung of flies, frogs from saltwort, gnats from tainted air, that is, from human breath.

Virgil says these are produced from the lifeless body of a draught animal, but wasps and hornets from the bodies of horses, and beetles from the bodies of donkeys. But note that bees that come from draught animals and buffaloes mate as flies do, though in their breeding they follow nearly the same nature as true bees. Honey should be gathered at the full moon, on a clear day. That droplets break off suddenly and spring back is a sign of inferiority; the proof of good quality, however, is that it be fragrant and, from something sweet, sticky and translucent; and good honey comes from new wax, while that from old wax is reddish, and good honey resembles gold; and good white honey is effective against ailments of the eyes and against tumors, and pure honey lies at the bottom.

Platearius: honey is hot in the first degree, dry in the second. Honey preserves and cleanses. It is used in medicines, and the bitterness of certain ingredients is tempered by its sweetness, and through the sweetness of that honey the medicines are drawn deeper into the affected parts of the body. It is mixed into electuaries and with powders, so that they keep longer and with greater efficacy. Against the cold humors of the stomach, honey should be given with warm water; it cleanses and also loosens. A wash of honey and water is also good for clearing the complexion. A suppository of honey roasted in a shell mixed with salt is also of great benefit to those with fevers.

Aristotle: older bees make sweeter honey than younger ones, because they have experience. Unskimmed honey causes bloating; drunk, it is good for the bites of a rabid dog and helps against dangerous wild beasts. Laodicean honey is bitter; whoever uses it goes mad, but grows calm again through sweating. Honey removes distaste and nausea. Emperors produce many offspring, but once these are grown, all the bees together, in agreement, kill the inferior ones, so that they do not scatter the swarm and stir up rebellion. In the manner of hens they brood their young. What first hatches is a white little worm. The emperor's own offspring, however, is at once honey-colored, formed from the choicest flower and in full abundance.

The spider weaves the finest webs from her own entrails, so as to catch flies. For she disembowels herself for the sake of catching flies so often that, entirely emptied, she eventually dies. For there is within spiders a certain woolly, fine substance that serves as sufficient material for the work. It is thought to be the female that weaves, the male that hunts. They give birth to little worms resembling eggs from their hindquarters; they lay these eggs among their webs. Spiders are also born without mating, from decay, namely from dust particles and the spittle of a man who has just eaten. In clear weather she weaves; in cloudy weather she does not weave. The spider does not hunt until she has recovered what was spent in the weaving, as the Experimentator says. A spider's web laid over a wound keeps it free from swelling and infection. She lives on juice, and so none of them ever dies of hunger. It is a sign of rain when spiders raise their webs higher. A spider lowers herself on a thread over the head of a serpent stretched out in the shade of a tree, and her bite has such power that it seizes the serpent's brain, even unto death.
A poultice made of flies, placed over the site of the pain, calms the swelling that comes from a spider's bite, as Aristotle says.
Michael Scot: the spider, sleeping, turns her back toward the ground and sleeps in the air, hanging from the threads she has woven; she turns her face toward the sky.

Toads, as the Book of Nature says, are counted among the other worms. It is a venomous reptile, of a pestilent appearance and filthy to the touch. It feeds on earth, and this by weight and measure; for however much it can gather into its front foot, that is its daily food. In Gaul there is a certain kind of toad that has a voice like a trumpet's; once carried away from that land, it loses its voice. It signifies those who wish to preach only in their own homeland.

Alexander: the toad gladly feeds on sage, whose root it sometimes poisons with its venom. For this reason a bed of sage should be fenced round with rue, whose dew is fatal to the toad. The same: a stone found in a toad's head, worn by a man, wards off the harm of poison. Also, from a toad burnt and reduced to ash, if left alone, a living toad is likewise generated, not only one but several. For it fears that the earth may fail as its food. In this it signifies the greedy and covetous.
The 'botrax' belongs to the toad family, having a frog's face. For the Greeks call the frog 'botraca,' as Isidore says.

As the Experimentator says, it is a venomous animal; hence, because of the amount of venom it contains, it swells up when touched. It fights with the spider and is overcome by her, and this because, when the spider repeatedly stings the 'botrax' and it cannot avenge itself, it becomes so bloated by swelling that it bursts in the middle. The 'botrax's' bite is exceedingly bad and cannot be healed. It nurtures a precious stone in its forehead, for which it is killed. There are two kinds of these stones, one white, and this is the better, the other dark and black, having a spot in the middle that faintly resembles a sky-blue color, and this kind, among the dark ones, is the better. This stone, taken as food, is said to heal a man's internal ailments, for it travels around the intestines and, once the cure is complete, passes out through the lower region. It must, however, be swallowed whole. The 'botrax' uses a special herb when its eye is blinded, and by this it recovers its sight. It is killed by rue, hates the light of the sun, walks by night, especially along paths worn by human footsteps. By day it rests hidden away; it flees the scent of a flowering vineyard. The stone it bears is said to counteract poison.
The silkworm, as Pliny says, is a little worm found in Assyria. Like spiders, it weaves webs for the luxury and finery of women, called 'bombycine' silk.

This worm, as Michael Scot says, spins a thread from its own mouth, in which it buries itself, so as to be reborn, after it has cast out everything foul, dark, and dung-like from its body; and then its body becomes translucent, when held up to the sun. Be like the silkworm, which eats nothing external once it is fully born.

The 'cincedula' is a kind of beetle, as Isidore says. It takes its name from the thing itself, since it glows while flying or walking. This worm, the size of a small fly, is seen in many parts of the world, but especially in Italy, flying by night. It shines like a spark in the darkness, so brightly that, if you saw it in the dark, you would think it a burst of sparks flying. This glow is chiefly in its tail, and shows more when it flies; but when it folds its wings, it is seen less. It is found endowed with a marvelous power; for if someone eats three of these worms, his lust will be entirely extinguished, and many who have tried this have confirmed it. Blessed, then, is the one who, shining in his works and in the fame of his virtues especially in the tail, that is, at the end of his life, dwells amid the darkness of the world, uncaught by that darkness: 'let your good works so shine before men,' and so on.

The 'cynomia' is a worm, as Isidore says, called in Greek the 'dog-fly'; for 'cynos' means dog in Greek. This fly is a bother to the ears of puppies, and although they often shake it off, it always flies back again, undeterred. But when it finds puppies too lazy to shake it off, it presses on relentlessly until it draws blood and inflicts a wound. By this it signifies the devil, whose suggestions, if someone carelessly receives into the ear of his mind instead of shaking them off, even to the point of consenting to sin or to pleasure, will inflict a wound. So then, as Abraham did, drive away the flies and winged things of evil thoughts, and this with a rod, which is the sign of the cross.

For it was with a staff that David went against Goliath, and with a staff that Jacob crossed the Jordan — that is, the onslaught of temptations and evil thoughts, which, according to the wise man, separate us from God.
Gnats, as the Book of Nature says, are the smallest of flying worms. They follow the breath of livestock, and especially that of man.
They sting sleeping creatures, as Adelinus says, with certain stingers, delivering a wound and pain as sharp as they are able.

The mosquito is a worm, as Isidore says, and takes its name from the sting by which it sucks blood. For it has a tube in its mouth like a goad, with which it bores into the flesh of animals to drink their blood.
As the Experimentator says, the mosquito loves the light, and so it sometimes burns itself at a flame.

Isidore: mosquitoes seek out sour things and flee sweet ones, as Pliny says. In this they resemble slanderers, who always busy themselves spreading the evil deeds of men and take no care to recount any good, according to that saying: 'their wine is the gall of dragons,' and so on.

Blister-beetles are worms bred from the moisture in the leaves at the tips of the branches of the ash or the aloe tree. They grow like caterpillars, but also fully develop wings and fly by day; at night, however, they gather into a single mass. These worms, of a green color, shine gold in the rays of the sun. Around the month of August they are gathered by night for use as a remedy and killed, submerged in vinegar. Once dead, doused in wine, they are placed on whatever part of the body one wishes, under a small wax vessel shaped like a cup, and, applied this way, they raise a burning blister. This blister, once pierced in several places with a golden needle or the sharp point of a straw, discharges harmful humors like a cautery, and its discharge is as effective over twenty days as an actual cautery is over a year.

Hornets, as Pliny says, live in caverns or underground. Their cells are six-sided; their wax, however, is web-like in texture. Their brood is uneven and irregular: one flies off, another lies in water, another remains a small worm. They feed on flesh; they grow at the full moon, and hide away in winter.

Authors say that a two-year-old child is killed by nine hornet stings. Hornets and wasps have no king as bees do, but are governed by their own separate authority. Hence it happens that they are exposed to many more dangers. Their honey is useless for human use; they produce harsh sounds and murmurs, and this especially in hollow places.
The caterpillar, as the Book of Nature says, is a long worm, spaced out with many feet, of varied color. It feeds on vegetables and the foliage of trees.

Around the month of September, doused with heavenly dew or rain, it is said suddenly to change color and shape, so that, having grown wings, it can fly, whereas before it crawled on countless feet, as the Experimentator says. A caterpillar passing over a man's skin stains it and leaves pustules behind, as a mark of venom, even though it is not potent enough to cause great harm.

The ant has a sense of smell, as Aristotle says, and this can be proven as follows: take sulphur and wild marjoram, and, once powdered, place them over their dwellings, and they will at once flee and abandon their homes. During the new moon they always cease working. Among all other animals, the ant alone grows stronger and increases with old age. They also work by night at the full moon, but cease during the new moon. We see the very stones worn down by their path, and a track made by their labor — so that no one may doubt what even the smallest persistence can accomplish in any matter. They carry out their dead and bury them, and this, among all animals, they do alone, except for man.

Ants, as Ambrose says, bite off the tips of the grain they have gathered so that it does not sprout again. If it becomes damp, they dry it in the sun, so that it does not begin to rot. They stop working during the new moon; they always labor by night as the moon waxes full. This creature alone grows stronger with age, and can even fly.

The 'formicaleon,' also called the 'myrmicoleon' by Adelinus, is explained from 'myrmex,' which means ant, and 'leo,' which means lion, as though 'the lion of ants.' This worm belongs to the ant family, but is much larger. While it is still small and weak in strength, it feigns peace through modesty; but once it has gained strength, power, and size of body, it scorns its former companions and now keeps company with the larger creatures. At last, growing bold with its increasing strength, it hides away out of sight and, after the manner of robbers, lies in wait for the ants laboring for the common good, and, like a brigand, seizes their burdens, or even kills and eats the ants themselves.
