In winter, however, when the ants have stored their food in the earth as though in a granary, the 'myrmicoleon,' who has prepared nothing for himself for use during the summer, plunders and destroys their labors. This kind of creature signifies hypocrites and deceivers within the cloister.

The snail is a kind of shelled creature, as the Experimentator says, named from mud ['limus'], because it is born in mud. It eats earth, has four horns, but two of them longer. While crawling it extends its horns, but as soon as it is touched, it draws them back in and folds itself up. In winter it hides, in spring it appears again. Its blood closes pores and effectively prevents hair from growing. Crushed and pounded, it heals abscesses in certain wounds.
The locust, as Gregory says, is named as though 'standing in place.' It has a head shaped somewhat like a horse's.

As the Experimentator says, locusts eat one another, the larger devouring the smaller. Their mouths are arranged in a quadrangular shape; they have a sting in place of a tail, and legs folded back beneath themselves. They are generated by the south wind, and die from the north wind and the northeast wind. They fatten more quickly on the blossoms of almond trees. They have a single intestine, full of filth and corruption. It is certain that they cross vast stretches of sea, through many days of continuous hunger — and it is a great marvel to us that, for the sake of foreign pasture, they know how to seek out places so distant. But what wonder is it, if a faithful man does the same for the sake of the food of eternal life and a hunger for the word of God? Locusts fly with such a rustling of wings that they are sometimes mistaken for other birds. The Parthians eat them as food. At the joints of their shoulder-blades they are said to have something like teeth, which, rubbing against each other, produce their rasping sound.

The fly, as the Book of Nature says, is a shameless creature; it loves the light and does not know how to move about in darkness; it turns most often and gladly toward warmth; it settles on damp places; it seeks out blood. It is a pest to every animal, and especially to man. Wherever it touches freshly cut flesh, worms soon follow, which corrupt the tainted meat, and this especially during the dog days.

Flies, drowned in water, like bees, sometimes revive after the space of an hour. They are generated from the decay of dung. They lay small worms, from which flies emerge, and these little worms are hard and black. Flies lack memory.

There is a kind of fly found in the regions of Cyprus, four-footed, as Pliny says, and winged, much larger than our flies. These are called 'pyrallis,' from 'pyr,' which means fire. For, living in furnaces, they fly unharmed right through the midst of the flames. And this is a marvel: for as long as it stays in the fire, it lives in the fire, but once it flies even a little way outside it, it dies.

Fleas are produced from heated dust, afterward tainted by moisture. The chief remedy against fleas is to rub the body with wormwood every evening, as Ambrose says. Fleas will not touch you, if you boil the herb wormwood with oil and anoint your body with it. A flea, split into two parts, revives.
Lice, as the Book of Nature says, are named from the number of their feet.

The chief remedy against these, as Philosophus says, is frequent washing of the body with sea water, or with strongly salted water, or quicksilver boiled for a long time with olive oil, and a belt dyed in it and worn, or butter mixed with quicksilver, and wearing garments soaked in it.

The frog fears everything that breathes; it suspects itself hated by everyone, as the Book of Nature says. In the month of August it can never open its mouth for any purpose of food, drink, or voice; and if you even try to open it with a stick or your hand, you will be able to open it only with difficulty. Frogs mate more by night than by day, and in this is noted a certain modesty about mating — apply this against those who mate indiscriminately and shamelessly, by night and by day alike. The tongue of a water-frog, if placed under the head of a sleeping person, makes him talk in his sleep and reveal secrets, as ancient folk wisdom obscurely puts it. A live frog given as food to a dog takes away its bark. There is also a small frog called the tree-frog; it climbs trees and rests there among the leaves. Sensing rain in the clouds by a natural instinct, it cries out loudly, announcing the coming flood, but at other times it scarcely ever sings. Thrown into the mouths of dogs, common folk believe it takes away their voice; this frog is green and small.

There is a small frog, as Pliny says, that lives mostly among reeds and grasses, mute and voiceless in the water; if this is accidentally swallowed by cattle, the cattle's bellies swell to an enormous size.

The leech is a worm living in water; it lacks bones, feet, and wings. When it has attached itself to a man's flesh, the more it is pulled, the more firmly it clings on, until it bursts. It draws out corrupted blood, and often brings death upon itself through excessive gorging, and so, in healing another, kills itself. In this it signifies those who, overcome by greed and rancor, tend to others' sins and, as a consequence, put their own souls to death. The leech, as the Experimentator says, should be pricked with thorns, brambles, and nettles, so that it vomits up the poison it has drawn from toads or other harmful creatures. It has a triangular mouth, hence it leaves a triangular wound.

The 'tappula' is a worm supported on four feet. This worm, having soles, walks boldly on water and does not fear the depths of a whirling current. It lives equally on land. On land it runs very swiftly, but even more so over the water, so that in a short time it crosses long stretches of water in a burst of speed; yet it pauses in its rush over the water and, tired, recovers its strength, and, although it runs over water, its body and feet stay dry. And even if you hold this worm forcibly under the waves for a long time, it does not become wet or die, but, once it returns to the surface, dry and unhindered, resumes its usual swift, undisturbed course.

The 'thamur,' or 'samer,' also called 'Solomon's worm,' takes and gets its name from the thing itself. This is reported in the Histories. This worm can fittingly bear the figure of Christ, whose blood is of such power that it softens even the adamantine hearts of men to compassion for Christ, and to contrition or knowledge of themselves.
The 'thamur' is a little worm, by which Solomon cut the stones of the Temple, as is said in the Historia Scholastica, and with whose blood the ostrich breaks glass, so as to free its chick.

[This worm] is of a golden color, as the Book of Nature says. When it sees a snake lying in the shade, it climbs up its tail, soothing it as though by stroking, and finally, with a bite, pierces to the very depths of its brain. So too sin first soothes, and afterward kills.

[This creature] is a worm born from the decay of grasses through the excessive moisture and heat of the season. It is a slow and bloated creature, full of thick blood. If you throw salt on it, nearly its whole body dissolves into nothing, and you will find little left of it but blood, which is useful as a remedy. Once the salt of wisdom is tasted, dissolution into devotion follows, and yet such a person seems to himself to be nothing.

Wood-worms, called by the Greeks the worms of timber, as Isidore says, are named from the fact that they eat their way along ['edant eundo']. Trees cut down at the proper season generate these worms. And note: the linden, the most delicate of trees, wherever its dry wood is kept, never produces worms from it, whereas every other kind of wood, except this one and the oak and a few others, produces worms in the western regions.

The clothes-moth is the worm of garments, as Isidore says, named from the fact that it holds on ['teneat']. This worm is generated from tainted air within garments and from the decaying moisture present in wool, and it settles there to such a degree that it gnaws it away.

The 'tarmus' is a worm, as Isidore says, born in cured pork fat. We call 'lardum' the fat of a pig lying directly beneath the skin, between the skin and the red flesh, and the word is taken from the Gallic language.
Wasps, as Pliny says, build their nests aloft out of mud. Their life centers around dung; they feed on flesh.
Wasps are sometimes produced from horse flesh, as Pope Clement says.

The name 'worm,' though it indeed applies to worms in general, is nonetheless properly and specifically given to that worm which is generated from pure, clean earth without any mixture of seed at all. It is with this worm that the hook is baited in the deceiving of fish. To this worm the Lord compares himself through the psalmist, when he says: 'I am a worm, and not a man' — and not without reason, since he was generated from the pure, clean flesh of his mother without the seed of corruption. Hence too the manna in the desert is said to have produced a worm.

The worms of Celidonia, on Augustine's testimony in the book On the City of God, are found in certain waters that boil naturally in the region of Celidonia. Just as a fish lives in cold water, so these live in hot, boiling water; once they leave the boiling water, they die at once in the cold.
